## Laws, wisdom, poetry, and letters are part of the action

| Material | Scene function | What must remain visible |
|---|---|---|
| Exodus case law; Leviticus; Numbers; Deuteronomy | V05-C10 tests a specific injured person against legal categories; C13 turns access, bodily condition, jubilee, and care into a practical dispute; C15 changes inheritance precedent; C16 makes farewell law an inherited responsibility. | Full legal enumeration remains unfinished. Source-era hierarchy and the author’s ethical revision must be compared openly, rather than presented as the same rule. |
| Proverbs | V06-C21–C22 compare memorable royal wisdom with the labour and justice practices of the state invoking it. | Attributed wisdom is not proof of an author or a guarantee of wise administration. Individual sayings still need selected destinations. |
| Job | V07-C17 gives the sufferer a consequential refusal to accept an invented explanation of guilt. | The different speeches, divine response, frame, and restoration cannot become one uniform maxim; losses remain real. |
| Psalms, Lamentations, Joel | V07-C14 gives displaced people a usable language of complaint; C18 preserves forms that an emergency archive would otherwise discard. | Speakers, genres, expressed desires, settings, and later uses remain distinct. A violent wish in a lament is not automatically an approved ethical command. |
| Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs | V07-C18 makes preservation of scepticism, ordinary delight, and love affect what the next generation can learn. | Their placement in an exile archive is a fictional transmission frame, not a certified composition date. The lovers remain persons rather than mandatory codes for cosmic entities. |
| Sirach and Wisdom of Solomon | V08-C12–C13 turn education and royal accountability into conflicts with visible recipients. | Useful insight does not erase restrictive social assumptions; personification does not establish entity identity. |
| Gospel teachings and parables | V09-C06 and C10 force listeners to act in specific debt, property, and care situations. | A parable may resist one fixed decoding. Distinct versions remain available in the Codex. |
| Acts and Pauline letters | V10-C03 changes food distribution; C08 gives recipients a response; C10 changes a meal; C12 delivers aid; C13 restores a letter’s social network; C14 measures whether a person actually becomes free. | Letter author, bearer, audience, later attribution, and institutional reuse are different evidence positions. |
| Catholic/general epistles and Hebrews | V10-C15–C19 place household restrictions, missing care, hospitality, office rules, and symbolic arguments before people affected by them. | Competing source voices are not forced into one speaker. No inherited contempt toward a people is accepted as a consequence of a ritual metaphor. |
| Apocalypses | V08-C17, V11-C01, and V11-C14 separate a vision’s initial pressure, transmission, later calculations, and continuing ethical demands. | Symbols do not automatically become physical map coordinates or reliable future dates. |

## The wider weave changes outcomes

The following are proposed fictional contributions, not claims that these encounters happened historically or that the traditions all teach one hidden doctrine.

| Chapter | Distinct contribution | Causal result |
|---|---|---|
| V11-C02 | The Gospel of Mary’s disputed witness and fragmentary survival. | A testimony remains available without invented missing pages being passed off as a recovery. |
| V11-C03 | Gnostic creation accounts retain their own entities and relationships. | A tempting but unsupported identity equation is held back. |
| V11-C04 | Manichaean and Zoroastrian terminology travels through a documented translation conflict. | Recoverable differences survive and later aid an identity investigation. |
| V11-C05 | A distinct Buddhist practice of attending to conditions changes an escalating dispute. | The coalition postpones retaliation and acts on a preventable cause. |
| V11-C06 | Hindu sources restore conflicting duties and situated argument to an abused quotation. | A commander loses an easy justification and must specify the actual obligations of a proposed intervention. |
| V11-C07 | Jain non-harm changes route planning. | A settlement survives because speed and resources are sacrificed. |
| V11-C08 | Daoist and Confucian participants remain distinct while correcting neglect and coercive hierarchy. | Infrastructure stays usable through a negotiated maintenance practice. |
| V11-C09 | Quranic testimony retains real disagreement about shared named figures. | A mistaken identity inference is withdrawn before it can compel a false reunion. |
| V11-C10 | A Sikh source practice of common service changes who works and receives. | The next coalition meeting redistributes standing through actual shared labour. |
| V11-C11 | Yoruba and distinct diaspora custodians retain local identity and interpretive custody. | A stolen identification is corrected instead of incorporated into a universal deity chart. |
| V11-C12 | A K’iche’ text’s transmission and custodians remain visible. | Access rules change because a public text is no longer treated as ownerless material. |
| V12-C05 and C11 | The earlier contributions supply different maps, relationships, evidence, and ethical constraints. | The modern investigation and intervention cannot succeed by removing the wider weave. |

These chapters use later reading and transmission frames when a source’s narrated time predates the surrounding volume. They do not imply every tradition originated after the New Testament. Other listed global traditions remain in the source catalogue without being falsely counted as fully dramatized here.

## Notes that travel with each paired chapter

The Codex must identify the passage and edition; distinguish narrated date from composition, surviving witness, and later reception; explain a custom or institution through relevant evidence; preserve important variants and missing text; and name where the fiction departs from its sources. A map should distinguish documented geography, source-tradition geography, and invented realm geometry. Numerical explanation must distinguish measurement, metaphor, and an invented story rule.

## Specific unresolved checks

- Lilith’s later traditions are not an omitted Genesis passage. Her independent cross-volume refuge history is a visible editorial proposal.
- Mother begins not lonely. FirstFlame’s loneliness belongs to him; any later grief in Mother must be earned in sequence.
- Firstborn fixedness versus capacity for learning remains a source conflict. A dissenter does not silently resolve it.
- Mother, Lilith, and Lily are not automatically identical. A framing dialogue does not establish pre-Garden embodiment or simultaneous bodies.
- Exodus 22:20 in NABRE corresponds to 22:21 in other numbering for the alien injunction; the version must travel with the locator.
- V11-C13 uses the Christian Apocalypse of Peter with Greek/Ethiopic witnesses and the Latin Visio Pauli, not the separately catalogued Nag Hammadi works with similar titles.
- Every broad source range still requires a passage inventory. An outline, catalogue, citation, or successful link check does not complete the adaptation.

# The Good Book: the twelve-volume series

An adult dark fantasy and dark comedy epic, moving through a biblical spine and an expanding world of religious testimony. The novels and their parallel Codex editions tell the same events. The Codex supplies the denser explanations, source differences, and historical context.

This is the complete first outline of the series, not a claim that every scripture has been adapted or that these proposed scenes are already approved prose. Historical traditions, the author’s cosmology, and fictional testimony remain distinguishable.

## 1. Before the Word

Before anyone can call a world good, someone has to live in it. Mother and FirstFlame face the difficulty of making company that can disagree with them. Their children inherit an unfinished creation, unequal knowledge, and the temptation to mistake making a thing for owning it.

**The central conflict:** Can creation become a relationship when its creators could instead demand obedience?

**Chapters**

1. **Before Anyone Asked** — The first unanswered invitation becomes a limit Mother elects to keep
2. **The First Warm Thing** — Warmth becomes inhabitable while the withheld blaze remains a responsibility
3. **The Space Between Yes and Yes** — Their first negotiated difference produces a place neither controls alone
4. **An Inventory of Nearly Everything** — The first archive preserves a disputed name instead of correcting its bearer
5. **The Child Who Would Not Shine** — Creation acquires a vacant post and a child whose future remains undecided
6. **Which Morning** — Appointments become possible without erasing incompatible ages
7. **Bread for Beings Without Mouths** — Creation's abundance becomes uneven, revisable, and answerable to recipients
8. **The Empty Place at the Count** — Loss enters the archive as an event that counting cannot reverse
9. **The Office of Keeping Things Good** — A protective institution survives only after surrendering its unlimited mandate
10. **Three Shadows and a Name** — A false identity claim fails without denying that one source may appear differently
11. **The Door That Opens Outward** — The first departure leaves an actual absence and a relationship that must travel
12. **The Word Was Not a Receipt** — Distinct beings enter history carrying permission to answer and responsibility to act
13. **Lilith Asks Who Is Speaking** — Lilith becomes an active recipient who preserves her own standing while creation remains temporally earlier

## 2. The Garden and the Refusal

A garden offers food, safety, and an answer to every question except who agreed to the arrangement. Lilith refuses an assigned place. Adam and Eve confront knowledge, dependence, and the cost of leaving. Beyond the gates, the first families discover that suffering does not automatically make people kinder.

**The central conflict:** What belongs to a person when shelter, identity, and obedience have been bundled into one contract?

**Chapters**

1. **Two Accounts of the Soil** — The Garden's archive begins with visible disagreement rather than a forged synthesis
2. **Lilith Declines the Arrangement** — An absent woman becomes a contested memory others will try to author
3. **Adam Names What Moves** — Naming becomes a fallible practice rather than a universal property deed
4. **A Person Across the Table** — The household's apparent harmony becomes a negotiation between persons
5. **The Question with Teeth** — The decision to seek knowledge becomes hers rather than the serpent's command
6. **What the Mouth Knows** — Knowledge enters the relationship before either has agreed how to bear it
7. **Where Are You Hiding** — The first shared crisis fractures trust before any formal sentence
8. **The Terms Nobody Negotiated** — Future interpreters inherit a record that cannot honestly make every suffering an obligation
9. **The Gate and the Ration** — Outside the Garden, divided food sustains an injured household without restoring its safety
10. **The Offering Nobody Explains** — Abel's death makes rivalry irreversible and leaves a survivor who cannot outsource responsibility
11. **A Mark Is Not an Acquittal** — Cain lives beyond the killing without being cleared of it
12. **The Names After Abel** — First families inherit a memory of refusal, work, and murder rather than a clean origin
13. **The Shelter Lilith Builds** — Lilith gains neighbours and material obligations beyond Adam's household; her refusal becomes a durable alternative

## 3. The Waters and the Scattering

Knowledge arrives with patrons attached. Enoch enters a dispute whose witnesses do not share a clock. Flood survivors preserve more than life: they preserve evidence, guilt, and the habits that made the catastrophe possible. A great building project promises reunion and creates a new argument over whose language counts.

**The central conflict:** Who gets to call a disaster a fresh start when its survivors still remember the cost?

**Chapters**

1. **The Teachers Arrive** — A useful craft enters the community alongside a public dispute over its teachers
2. **Iron for the Harvest** — A practical benefit survives while the smith incurs a dangerous debt
3. **The Mouths of the Great** — The settlement loses its comforting forecast and gains evidence for collective complaint
4. **Enoch Carries the Complaint** — Enoch becomes a witness whom neither side can comfortably claim
5. **A Tour Without a Map** — The archive gains a navigable testimony that admits what Enoch could not measure
6. **The Sentence Reaches Home Late** — Those affected can name the warning's lateness instead of being blamed for not complying
7. **An Ark Is a Selection** — The ark becomes both a refuge and evidence of unavoidable exclusions
8. **The Door from the Other Side** — A second survival memory persists outside the ark family's account
9. **The Bird Does Not Explain** — The household returns to land cautiously rather than declaring the world repaired
10. **The Vineyard After the Promise** — The household preserves a fracture beside the covenant and cannot make prejudice a factual inheritance
11. **The Tower's Common Language** — Cooperation exposes its coercive language policy before the project loses cohesion
12. **What the Roads Carry** — Scattered peoples enter new homelands with distinct memories and a future need for translation
13. **The People the Ark Did Not Name** — A scattered community survives owing Lilith no perpetual allegiance; the first refuge is irretrievably lost

## 4. The Houses of Covenant

The promise of a future passes through tents, wombs, wells, bargains, and graves. Abraham's household grows into competing histories told by people with unequal power. Hagar and Sarah have different reasons to fear the same promise. Joseph eventually learns that feeding a nation can save his family while building the machinery that will later confine it.

**The central conflict:** Who pays for a family's promised destiny?

**Chapters**

1. **Leave What Can Find You** — A migrant household begins carrying a covenant it must repeatedly interpret
2. **The Price of Calling Her Sister** — The household leaves safer materially but less able to call its conduct innocent
3. **The Well Beyond the Tent** — Hagar's account becomes an independent line of memory that the household cannot own
4. **Laughter at the Door** — The promise reaches the household bearing Sarah's doubt rather than erasing it
5. **How Many Would Be Enough** — The record preserves a challenge to collective punishment from within the covenant relationship
6. **The Door in Sodom** — Escape leaves a fractured family whose injuries cannot be hidden by the rescue account
7. **Water for the Child** — An independent household survives beyond Abraham's control
8. **The Knife and the Answer** — The interrupted sacrifice leaves a father-son relationship that must answer for what nearly happened
9. **A Grave Bought in Public** — The household's first secured place is a grave rather than the promised kingdom
10. **Rebekah Answers for Herself** — The next household begins with a departure attributable to Rebekah's decision
11. **The Bowl and the Blessing** — A meal becomes a disputed transfer that poisons the brothers' future
12. **The Ladder on Borrowed Ground** — Jacob carries a sacred encounter that does not clear his earlier deceit
13. **Wages in the Household** — The household grows through rival loyalties that no patriarch fully directs
14. **The Name after Wrestling** — Reunion interrupts vengeance but does not erase the brothers' separate futures
15. **The Brother in the Pit** — Family betrayal sends Joseph into a different system of vulnerability and power
16. **The Granary and the Throne** — The family survives in Egypt inside a strengthened state that later rulers can exploit
17. **A Promise for the Unchosen** — A fragile aid route survives outside the covenant households and later offers an alternative to state dependence

## 5. The Bondage and the Liberation

A river, a basket, and a fugitive begin a liberation that will outgrow all three. Leaving Egypt ends one form of bondage and exposes the difficulty of living together without its machinery. The wilderness becomes a place of food queues, sanctuary disputes, failed leadership, and arguments over the terms of freedom.

**The central conflict:** Can a movement against coercion recognize coercion in its own rules?

**Chapters**

1. **The Midwives' Answer** — A continuity of ordinary care survives before any public liberator arrives
2. **The Basket Changes Houses** — The child's survival joins households whose power and loyalties remain unequal
3. **The Fire with an Assignment** — Moses returns with a task, a partner, and doubts that do not vanish at departure
4. **Bricks without the Straw** — The movement must answer to worsened working conditions instead of treating resistance as instant relief
5. **The Contest over Signs** — The dispute spreads beyond elite performance into households losing water, food, and trust
6. **The Night No House Forgets** — Liberation carries an adjacent grief that its triumphal telling cannot erase
7. **The Song on the Far Bank** — A public memory of liberation forms with women's leadership visible inside it
8. **Daily Bread Does Not Store Well** — Provision becomes a contested daily practice rather than a permanent miracle exemption
9. **One Judge Is a Queue** — Judgement gains local access while exposing the need to review delegated authority
10. **The Mountain and the Case** — Freedom's founding law acquires an unresolved case that later interpreters must face
11. **The People Who Make the Sanctuary** — The sanctuary becomes a made and maintained place whose workers retain names
12. **The Calf and the Missing Leader** — The institution survives a rupture only by carrying evidence of leadership failure
13. **Outside until Evening** — The community must distinguish bodily condition, ritual status, and moral blame in a lived dispute
14. **The Census and the Dissent** — The wilderness generation becomes more than an army's failed itinerary
15. **The Daughters Bring a Case** — A named exception changes legal precedent while later conditions reveal its remaining limits
16. **The Mountain Moses Cannot Cross** — A successor generation approaches the land with unfinished duties rather than a leader's guaranteed ending
17. **The Stranger at Lilith's Fire** — A mixed refuge preserves lives and testimony outside the victorious community's membership system

## 6. The Land and the Crowns

The land is already inhabited. Conquest accounts, local memories, marriage bargains, and rescue stories collide before the demand for a king turns them into a national story. Ruth seeks a future in the margins. Saul and David discover what a crown can license; Solomon builds a magnificent answer to questions he cannot settle.

**The central conflict:** When a people wants safety badly enough to crown someone, what powers have they actually granted?

**Chapters**

1. **Rahab Bargains for a Household** — An outsider's negotiated rescue complicates the claim that the city's people form one undifferentiated enemy
2. **Carrying Stones across Water** — A national monument carries a child's question into later retelling
3. **The Walls and the Neighbours** — The conquest begins with irreducible evidence of those whose city was lost
4. **The Lot Falls** — A victory explanation acquires a documented boundary dispute over accountability
5. **The Treaty with Worn Shoes** — A deceptive survival treaty creates lasting service obligations and a contested debt
6. **Land on the Ledger** — The allotment archive exposes unresolved coexistence beneath territorial claims
7. **The Farewell at Shechem** — A departing leader leaves a compact whose later breaches can be named concretely
8. **Deborah's Two Accounts** — Public memory cannot entirely remove Deborah and Jael from the victory it claims
9. **The Snare after Gideon** — A rescuer's monument becomes evidence that success can cultivate the next dependency
10. **The Bramble Offers Shade** — The reign begins under a public warning its supporters cannot claim never to have heard
11. **The Daughter Hears the Vow** — The vow's cost belongs to an identified daughter rather than a father's heroic résumé
12. **The Strong Man's Audience** — Exceptional strength ends with an aftermath that cannot be reduced to the performer's legend
13. **The Message Made from a Body** — Civil war loses its claim to have repaired the violation that initiated its summons
14. **Ruth at the Edge of the Field** — A foreign widow enters the lineage while her practical agency remains visible
15. **Hannah's Child and the People's King** — Monarchy begins with a warning that later rulers cannot call an unforeseen objection
16. **Saul Counts What Obedience Costs** — Royal authority fractures from prophetic endorsement without simply disappearing
17. **David Refuses the Convenient Killing** — David gains a model of restraint that his later reign will be judged against
18. **The City and the Ark** — The city acquires a religious centre that is also an argument over who owns public meaning
19. **Bathsheba Does Not Disappear** — David's reign carries an injury that confession alone cannot repay
20. **Tamar's Unanswered Petition** — The succession crisis exposes a household that can wage war but cannot answer its harmed member
21. **The Judgement Everyone Repeats** — Royal wisdom gains a public test that later administrative conduct must also satisfy
22. **The Temple's Unpaid Ledger** — The kingdom's splendour reaches completion carrying the costs that will help divide it
23. **No Crown over the Refuge** — Families evade conscription, but Lilith loses a defensible home and the political patronage that could rebuild it

## 7. The Kingdoms and the Exile

The kingdom breaks along the lines its monuments concealed. Prophets, debtors, courtiers, and displaced families argue over what is happening while empires collect payment. When the sanctuary falls, grief becomes a struggle over memory: whether to confess, accuse, endure, or refuse the explanations offered by survivors with authority.

**The central conflict:** How can people answer for their own failures without accepting every conqueror's explanation of their suffering?

**Chapters**

1. **The Heavier Yoke** — The kingdom divides at the point where royal image defeats practical hearing
2. **The Widow's Last Meal** — Survival binds two vulnerable households without making hunger a trivial test
3. **Naboth's Field** — The palace acquires land alongside evidence that its acquisition was an abuse
4. **Elisha and the Debtor's Oil** — A household escapes seizure through collective practical work rather than a lecture on patience
5. **Amos at the Market** — A prophetic accusation becomes a visible dispute over who profits from ordinary commerce
6. **Whose Marriage Becomes a Nation** — The prophecy remains forceful while its human subject gains a claim the metaphor cannot consume
7. **Isaiah's Sign in a Besieged City** — The city receives a hope that later readers must distinguish from its first political circumstance
8. **Micah's Complaint at the Boundary** — Justice becomes an argument about fields and homes rather than the excellence of ceremonial offerings
9. **Nineveh in Two Registers** — The archive gives victims room to seek judgement while withholding a monopoly on compassion
10. **The Watch Post and the Question** — Faithful testimony includes an unresolved challenge to the means of judgement
11. **Josiah Finds the Book** — Renewal acquires both a textual centre and a debate over the power used in its name
12. **Jeremiah Buys a Future** — An archive of future obligation survives the collapse of immediate possession
13. **The Last Stores of Jerusalem** — The city's fall enters the series through exhausted households as well as royal chronology
14. **Lament Refuses the Explanation** — The displaced acquire a language that can address loss without finishing its meaning
15. **Edom at the Closed Road** — Exile's geography acquires a remembered betrayal that later repair must address specifically
16. **Ezekiel beside the Foreign River** — Hope travels beyond the lost sanctuary without pretending displacement never happened
17. **Job Will Not Sign the Confession** — The wisdom archive preserves a harmed person's refusal to validate a convenient explanation
18. **The Song Kept beside the Questions** — The portable library retains reasons to live as well as instructions for survival
19. **The Names Lilith Cannot Carry Alone** — Lilith relinquishes exclusive access while a dispersed memory network outlives the loss of any one sanctuary

## 8. The Return and the Hidden Years

Return does not mean everyone comes home to the same place. Builders, displaced spouses, court survivors, healers, and insurgents attempt different forms of continuity. Esther, Judith, and Tobit belong to different kinds of telling, and their differences remain visible. Resistance hardens into institutions as new empires arrive.

**The central conflict:** Who is allowed to belong to a restored community, and who disappears from the story of its restoration?

**Chapters**

1. **The Permission to Return** — Return begins as a partial migration rather than the restoration of every exile
2. **The Foundation and the Old Voices** — The rebuilt centre carries visible continuity without pretending to reproduce the lost building
3. **The Wall and the Debt** — Defence acquires an obligation to the people it claims to defend
4. **The Household Outside the Assembly** — The return narrative retains the people expelled by its account of belonging
5. **Malachi at the Offering Table** — The restored cult is measured against ordinary conduct rather than its successful reopening
6. **Esther Learns the Palace's Clock** — A concealed identity becomes an instrument of intervention rather than a private shelter
7. **Mordecai Cannot Unsigned the Order** — Deliverance enters communal memory alongside unresolved questions about retaliation and imperial procedure
8. **Tobit's Unpaid Burial** — A received diaspora tale makes piety answerable to those sharing its material risks
9. **Sarah Names the Fear** — The healing tale ends with a household formed through shared vulnerability rather than a cursed-woman label
10. **Judith Challenges the Deadline** — The community's future shifts from passive countdown to a woman's accountable intervention
11. **The Head and the Song** — The tale's deliverer remains distinct from the institution her act preserved
12. **Ben Sira's Classroom** — A wisdom tradition enters the plot through contested education rather than unquestioned maxims
13. **Wisdom Faces the Ruler** — A transmitted teaching becomes grounds to contest official self-justification
14. **Resistance on the Day of Rest** — Resistance develops a precedent that will later need limits of its own
15. **The Lamps after the Siege** — Rededication establishes a living practice of remembrance rather than an untouched past
16. **What the Martyr's Family Owes** — The community can remember courage without conscripting every vulnerable person into the same death
17. **Daniel's Later Readers** — Apocalyptic expectation gains a disciplined reader who can act without claiming a final calendar
18. **The Hidden Years Are Inhabited** — The Gospel world opens as a populated network of schools, households, sanctuaries, and hopes
19. **The Page They Call a Monster** — The archive keeps its history of vilification and gains a witness it can no longer describe only from outside

## 9. The Word in Flesh

Into a landscape already full of saviours, creditors, priests, soldiers, and exhausted families comes a life that refuses to stay in the category assigned to it. Teaching and healing change daily obligations before they provoke public crisis. The execution leaves actual wounds. What follows reaches the reader through witnesses whose differences matter.

**The central conflict:** What does good news require from the living when it offers them no permission to forget the dead?

**Chapters**

1. **Mary Receives an Impossible Future** — An incarnation story begins with a woman's response rather than an abstraction acquiring a body
2. **Two Roads to a Birth** — The reader enters the infancy traditions with visible witness boundaries and no fabricated historical certainty
3. **John by the River** — The river becomes a place where ethical demands precede endorsement of a coming figure
4. **The Offers in the Wilderness** — The ministry begins with limits its later supporters will be tempted to bypass
5. **The People Who Leave Work** — Discipleship gains a material account of care beyond the named followers
6. **The Teaching Meets a Debt** — The sermon becomes a changed relationship with remaining costs, not merely admired language
7. **The Crowd and the Interrupted Journey** — One interrupted journey leaves two households changed without ranking their claims by status
8. **Water across the Boundary** — A marginal encounter becomes a community's independent investigation
9. **Who Is Welcome at the Table** — The household loses prestige with some neighbours and gains an altered practice of belonging
10. **The Story That Would Not Behave** — A familiar story becomes an inconvenient demand the listener can no longer merely quote
11. **Enough to Feed and Not to Rule** — The crowd is fed and the movement acquires a dispute over what the gift authorizes
12. **Peter Names What He Cannot Command** — The disciple gains a name for the relationship without gaining authority over its course
13. **Martha Meets the Delay** — Lazarus's return intensifies both attachment and opposition while the family keeps its memory of grief
14. **The City Hears the Arrival** — The public confrontation acquires ordinary witnesses whose needs exceed the spectacle
15. **The Last Table Is Still a Table** — A repeated future rite begins in a particular household with betrayal and care still unresolved
16. **The Garden after the Supper** — The arrest proceeds with fear, abandonment, and deliberate limits on retaliation visible
17. **The Hearing and the Courtyard** — A future witness begins with a failure he cannot honestly edit out
18. **The Execution Has Witnesses** — The execution leaves bereaved people, implicated institutions, and an injury no later claim can render unreal
19. **Mary Finds the Account Unfinished** — Resurrection testimony enters circulation through a witness who must still be heard
20. **Breakfast after the End** — The companions leave with responsibility and disagreement instead of a fully installed religion
21. **Lilith Does Not Speak for the Women** — The women retain independent accounts and the witness network gains protection without a replacement narrator

## 10. The Witnesses and the Empires

The story continues in kitchens, prisons, workshops, argument, and post. Acts and the letters become events happening to particular people rather than an uninterrupted speech from above. A collection can keep a distant household alive; a sentence can also protect a hierarchy. The recipients get to answer back.

**The central conflict:** How do communities preserve a witness without granting every interpreter ownership of it?

**Chapters**

1. **The Languages in the Street** — The movement begins its public life through translation that reaches distinct listeners
2. **The Common Purse and the Fear** — Common goods acquire a transparency practice and an unresolved warning about coercive holiness
3. **The Widows Count Themselves** — New service roles emerge because overlooked recipients name the failure
4. **The Reader on the Road** — A traveller carries the witness beyond the messenger's ongoing supervision
5. **The Man the Household Fears** — A transformed adversary enters relation without an entitlement to immediate trust
6. **Peter Enters Another House** — Admission practices change because a concrete household exceeds the existing rule
7. **The Council and the Missing Chairs** — A negotiated letter travels outward with relief and continuing interpretive disputes
8. **Galatia Answers the Letter** — A disputed letter becomes a communal choice about responsibility rather than a remote command alone
9. **The Night Shift Waiting for the End** — Expectation remains livable without making daily responsibility a betrayal of hope
10. **The Meal in Corinth** — A ritual's meaning changes when the hungry participant becomes its measure of failure
11. **The Body with Different Voices** — Charismatic activity gains a limit based on the people meant to receive it
12. **The Collection Reaches a Door** — A distant theological relation becomes food and obligations in a particular household
13. **Phoebe Carries an Argument** — The Roman communities receive an argument whose social network resists reduction to isolated maxims
14. **Onesimus at the Threshold** — The correspondence cannot be called a completed liberation until the person's condition changes
15. **The Household Code Meets the Household** — The reader sees the distance between a household ideal and the dependent person's actual options
16. **James Asks Where the Coat Went** — The assembly's claimed faith becomes testable through a completed act of care
17. **The Office and the Silenced Teacher** — An institutional dispute preserves the teacher's contribution and the contested restrictions separately
18. **Three Letters and a Guest** — A household learns that welcome and boundary-setting can both protect relation
19. **The Curtain in the Argument** — The community can receive the exhortation without converting difference into inherited inferiority
20. **The Shore before the Empire** — The movement enters the imperial centre through shared dependence and unfinished testimony
21. **The Refuge Refuses a Creed Test** — The network survives less comfortably and remains available to those the new institutional boundaries exclude

## 11. The Unveilings and the Inheritances

The end of one book becomes the beginning of its custody. Visions survive copying, translation, institutional conflict, destruction, and care. The wider religious weave becomes causally active through custodians who contribute different disciplines of remembrance, accountability, hospitality, and refusal. Their sources remain distinct even when the fictional history intersects.

**The central conflict:** Can an inheritance remain alive when its keepers stop claiming to possess the whole truth?

**Chapters**

1. **The Beast in the Ledger** — The apocalypse becomes a challenge to lived imperial relations before a timetable for distant readers
2. **Mary's Interrupted Account** — A disputed woman's testimony survives without invented pages being passed off as recovered text
3. **Sophia in the Disputed Beginning** — The cosmology gains a challenging witness that can alter a proposal without being silently absorbed
4. **The Translator at the Crossing** — A translation preserves a recoverable disagreement that later remembering can use
5. **The Bowl and the Chain of Causes** — The coalition postpones a retaliatory operation and discovers a preventable cause it can actually change
6. **The Charioteer Is Not a Shortcut** — The intervention plan must name its particular obligations instead of hiding behind an imported cosmic mandate
7. **The Route That Spares a Settlement** — A threatened settlement survives because non-harm changes logistics rather than only the group's language
8. **The Canal and the Unforced Turn** — A route remains open because distinct approaches correct each other's practical excesses
9. **Mary in Another Testimony** — A mistaken identity inference is withdrawn, preventing an attempted reunion of persons the evidence cannot equate
10. **The Kitchen Has No Elevated Table** — The coalition changes who works, who receives, and who can speak at its next meeting
11. **The Names across the Water** — A stolen identification is corrected and an archive returns interpretive control to its custodians
12. **The Book with More Than One Keeper** — A supposedly ownerless myth becomes an accountable archive that changes the coalition's access rules
13. **The Archive Survives Its Benefactor** — The wider history becomes recoverable without one institution controlling every surviving witness
14. **The Ending Left Open** — Living archives pass into the modern era with a promise of renewal and an explicit ledger of costs not erased
15. **Lilith Leaves Her Name with the Keepers** — Modern remembering becomes possible through independent records rather than one overwhelming identity proclamation

## 12. The Return of Names

Modern lives encounter records that know more names than any one witness can bear. Selected material from The Unraveling returns through a disciplined reconstruction of identity and consequence. Remembering does not make anyone entitled to another person. The final work is practical: living together after revelation, recording what changed, and repairing what cannot simply be undone.

**The central conflict:** What should someone do after recovering a name that seems large enough to swallow everybody else's?

**Chapters**

1. **An Ordinary Place Develops an Exception** — Modern remembering begins with a limited witness and a damaged ordinary place
2. **June Asks What Happened First** — Lily gains a method and a collaborator rather than a compulsory story about herself
3. **The Ward Does Not Owe a Miracle** — Recovery practice gains a real consent boundary and a repair obligation that power cannot cancel
4. **Yuna Declines the Role** — The coalition must protect a young person's agency instead of treating potential as conscription
5. **The Coalition Brings Its Own Maps** — Distinct contributions from earlier transmissions become necessary to solve the modern route and identity problem
6. **The Garden Is Not a Memory You Own** — Recovered identity becomes a supported but bounded relation instead of an entitlement to other people's pasts
7. **The Contract behind the Immortality** — The coalition identifies a specific exploitative mechanism and the people owed repair
8. **The Firstborn's Preservation Order** — The conflict divides an institution internally and saves witnesses needed for later accountability
9. **Eve Offers the Third Door** — An adversary becomes a limited collaborator without absolution or mandatory reconciliation
10. **Mother Arrives without Replacing Anyone** — The foundational presence returns as a participant in repair rather than an eraser of personhood
11. **The New Passage Has an Old Cost** — A new passage works, but its users inherit concrete duties to people whose costs remain
12. **Lily and Lilith Keep Two Places** — Recovered identity enlarges relation while Lily's ordinary history and Lilith's long commitments remain separately accountable
13. **What Lilith and Eve Build Next** — A repaired refuge exists because the women cooperate; neither must surrender her account for their relationship to change
14. **The Names at the Table** — The series ends in a changed world where care continues and nobody must disappear for the ending to count

## How to read the supporting books

Read the novel straight through. Use the Codex when a disputed account, unfamiliar custom, location, word, or mathematical idea invites a closer look. Different traditions are allowed to disagree. Their differences can matter to the plot without being presented as established historical proof.

The ending must account for what people lived through. Remembering, reconciliation, or a changed worldline cannot erase injury, turn coercion into consent, or require forgiveness.

# What returns from The Unraveling V2

The new series is not a wholesale reprint or an automatic adoption of every older rule. V2 supplies an awakening crisis, a difficult friendship, Lilith and Eve’s conflict, institutional opponents, the possibility of another route, and an aftermath that matters. Its 50 chapter hooks, prologue, and epilogue each have a disposition below.

The exact source file is preserved. The core identity sections, supporting cast, and complete chapter-hook outline were inspected for this map; not every prose sample and system section was reread.

| V2 unit | Title | New destination | Reuse decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| U2-PROLOGUE | Prologue | V12-C01 | Ordinary commercial place meets extraordinary danger; transaction and identity mechanics remain proposals. |
| U2-C01 | Three Days Dead | V12-C01 | Keep the disturbing identity question as a candidate; do not treat a speaking alternate body as disposable or infer identity from appearance. |
| U2-C02 | The Dice Don't Care | V12-C02 | Retain untrained power and social consequence; reject involuntary exposure being treated as harmless rent-payment comedy. |
| U2-C03 | The Girl Who Sees Too Much | V12-C02 | Retain June and route perception; her all-history identity claim remains a claim to test, not narrator-certified truth. |
| U2-C04 | The Support Group from Hell | V12-C02 | Retain a flawed support network and camaraderie; no automatic import of game ontology or min-max language. |
| U2-C05 | Meat and Memory | V12-C03 | Retain the recovery setting and horror of damaged memory; patients remain persons with interests, not empty bodies without worthwhile lives. |
| U2-C06 | The First Garden (Memory) | V12-C06 | Retain refusal and recovered Garden evidence; distinguish memory strength from complete authority. |
| U2-C07 | The Firstborn's Jealousy | V12-C08 | Retain conflict within claimed luminous authority; Firstborn ontology and fixedness remain open. |
| U2-C08 | The Price of Power | V12-C02 | Memory-sacrifice mechanics require separate approval and ethical accounting; no automatic advancement tariff adopted. |
| U2-C09 | The Threshold Tourist | V12-C02 | Retain difficult passage and costly guidance as candidates; memory trade does not become a default valid bargain. |
| U2-C10 | A Thousand Lives | V12-C06 | Retain an alternate-life challenge if worldline rules support it; no compulsory absorption of another person. |
| U2-C11 | Malcolm Thorne (Boss Fight 1) | V12-C07 | Retain Thorne and the private continuity bargain; his spouse requires an independent personhood and treatment account. |
| U2-C12 | The First Time She Fucks Up | V12-C03 | Retain failed-help accountability and continuing repair; do not present power or remorse as competence. |
| U2-C13 | Sex and the Singular Woman | V12-C14 | Retain adult tenderness and ordinary companionship as a craft reference only; this outline does not import the sexual set piece. |
| U2-C14 | The Heir of Eden | V12-C09 | Retain an Eve/Architect discovery as a proposed correspondence; earlier obedient-Eve simplification must be reconciled with her full agency. |
| U2-C15 | The Coalition Forms | V12-C05 | Retain a coalition whose members change the solution; cultural locations and claimed ages require evidence or explicit fiction labels. |
| U2-C16 | The Strip Mall of Eden | V12-C06 | Retain the collision of mundane place and deep memory as a possibility; New Jersey as actual Eden is not adopted geography. |
| U2-C17 | Adam Apologizes | V12-C06 | Retain apology without entitlement to forgiveness; no automatic adoption of exact reincarnation duration. |
| U2-C18 | War Crimes of the Divine | V12-C08 | Retain evidence of institutional erasure; lived timelines cannot be retroactively made nonexistent by narrative convenience. |
| U2-C19 | The Architect's Proposal | V12-C09 | Retain a justified grievance confronting an unacceptable universal remedy. |
| U2-C20 | The Siege of Detroit | V12-C08 | Retain a choice to protect people over pursuing a foe; exact Detroit siege design and casualty figures are not imported. |
| U2-C21 | The Price of Heroism | V12-C11 | Retain aftermath and public fallibility; source figure 847 is not adopted without a scene and casualty-accounting basis. |
| U2-C22 | Into the Reflection | V12-C06 | Retain examination of disowned motives; shadow integration must not become identity merger of independent persons. |
| U2-C23 | The Real Enemy | V12-C08 | Retain self-interested institutional conduct; avoid making every Firstborn morally identical. |
| U2-C24 | The Mother's Voice | V12-C10 | Retain Mother as a distinct foundational presence; she is not initially lonely or merely the solution to Father. |
| U2-C25 | The Crown Below | V12-C11 | Topology and lost-biome status require world reconciliation; no unearned geometric proof from imagery. |
| U2-C26 | The Longest Night | V12-C11 | Retain an intervention deadline only after actual clock and consequence rules are specified. |
| U2-C27 | Sister to Sister | V12-C13 | Retain direct confrontation between women with separate accounts and independent choices. |
| U2-C28 | The Third Option | V12-C09 | Retain the search beyond a false binary; the third route must be prepared by earlier causes, not invented as an effortless solution. |
| U2-C29 | The Ascent to Crown | V12-C11 | Retain a difficult traversal as a possible action sequence; reject mandatory total assimilation and unpriced power escalation. |
| U2-C30 | Waking the Flame | V12-C10 | Retain the demand for creator responsibility; a conversation does not guarantee a cure or universal compliance. |
| U2-C31 | The Expansion | V12-C11 | Retain bounded expansion as a candidate; affected beings, costs, and access must be accounted for. |
| U2-C32 | Eve's Choice | V12-C09 | Retain Eve choosing a future without forced forgiveness from those she harmed. |
| U2-C33 | The Morning After | V12-C11 | Retain material and social consequences of changed conditions after spectacle. |
| U2-C34 | Eve Joins the Coalition (Reluctantly) | V12-C13 | Retain accountable coexistence; remorse is not a substitute for those harmed retaining their claims. |
| U2-C35 | The Firstborn Strike Back | V12-C08 | Retain internal institutional dissent; source conflict over capacity to change must be resolved first. |
| U2-C36 | The Mother Returns | V12-C10 | Retain Mother returning in distinct relation; particular appearance remains an artistic proposal, not a race claim about divinity. |
| U2-C37 | The Real Trinity | V12-C10 | Retain plurality and a widened relational frame; do not silently replace every tradition with a compulsory identity equation. |
| U2-C38 | The First New Biome | V12-C11 | Retain creating a habitable refuge; numbered-biome count is inconsistent across V2 and remains unadopted. |
| U2-C39 | Years Pass | V12-C14 | Retain time passing with changed practices; exact three-year duration remains to be reconciled. |
| U2-C40 | The Last Firstborn | V12-C08 | Retain the possibility of leaving an office; Lucifer identification and inability-to-change claims require comparison. |
| U2-C41 | The Hollow Healed | V12-C11 | Retain continuing care without annihilation; do not equate a clinical condition with cosmic evil or promise that care alone cures it. |
| U2-C42 | Children of the New Age | V12-C14 | Retain a next generation with its own choices; do not assume inherited perception establishes superior standing. |
| U2-C43 | What Eve Built | V12-C13 | Retain Eve building actual repair capacity; the people receiving care retain agency and may refuse her involvement. |
| U2-C44 | The Axis Complete | V12-C14 | Retain an experienced wholeness as personal meaning; eight, twelve, and thirteen realm counts require reconciliation. |
| U2-C45 | The Weight of Being | V12-C14 | Retain ordinary identity after a defining conflict; victory cannot dictate who someone must become. |
| U2-C46 | Adam's Farewell | V12-C14 | Retain Adam accepting a boundary and relinquishing pursuit; exact death/reincarnation mechanics are not adopted. |
| U2-C47 | June's Goodbye (Temporary) | V12-C14 | Retain June choosing an independent journey; friendship survives an end to permanent availability. |
| U2-C48 | The First Flame Speaks (Finally) | V12-C10 | Retain FirstFlame speaking with accountability; gratitude cannot replace outstanding apology or repair. |
| U2-C49 | The Garden Opens | V12-C14 | Retain an open refuge whose ethics are enacted; welcome cannot become coerced entry or universal personal access. |
| U2-C50 | Home | V12-C14 | Retain a return to ordinary place and pleasure; do not copy the source closing line or require a clean emotional reset. |
| U2-EPILOGUE | A New Spark Wakes | V12-C14 | Life and future choices continue; do not repeat death as a mandatory awakening mechanism. |

The destinations are selection and development points. Several old episodes may contribute to one new chapter; a destination does not mean all their scenes have already been written or retained. The broader source catalogue separately tracks the other legacy collections.

# After “Before Anyone Asked”

This short reference contains only information available through the first novel chapter. The full planning atlas and indexes discuss later events.

| Entry | What the chapter establishes |
|---|---|
| The Mother | A presence holding possibility before the First Flame's awakening. She does not begin lonely. Her attempts to welcome him can fail. |
| The First Flame | A waking presence who does not yet recognise the Mother. He seeks company and begins to discover the effect of his own force. |
| The dark | The setting of the encounter and the Mother's presence; its lack of light does not establish emptiness or evil. |
| The shelter | A place the Mother shapes to receive an extension of the Flame. Her movement is mistaken for an independent answer. It breaks when he flares. |
| The fragment | A nonliving trace of the failed shelter. It has a smooth face, a ridged face, and a crack. The Flame eventually sustains warmth against it. |
| The unanswered interval | The space of an invitation whose response the Mother does not manufacture. |
| Time | The chapter establishes an order of experiences. It assigns no years, seconds, or universal clock. |

The final warmth leaves the crack intact. The Flame's care is a beginning, and his recognition of the Mother has still not occurred.

The [paired Codex entry](/codex-apockalypsis/library/codex-volume-01-01-the-unanswered-interval) adds commentary and historical comparisons. Those comparisons discuss this edition's adaptation, not an authenticated account of the physical beginning of the universe.

# Finding sources and reading their status

The source catalogue identifies 260 records. Its biblical baseline is complete at the book-identity level: 39 Old Testament and 27 New Testament books. It also registers major additional works, manuscript collections, and specific comparative families. Some records are components of another record, so 260 is neither a count of independent ancient books nor a claim to encompass every religion.

| Family | Records | Stable ID prefix |
|---|---:|---|
| Biblical baseline | 66 | `SRC-BIB-` |
| Major additional books and components | 29 | `SRC-DC-` |
| Jewish pseudepigrapha and reception | 30 | `SRC-JP-` |
| Dead Sea Scrolls works and collections | 13 | `SRC-DSS-` |
| Nag Hammadi work identities and fragments | 46 | `SRC-NH-` |
| Other Christian apocrypha and Coptic collections | 29 | `SRC-CA-` |
| Comparative traditions and discovery families | 47 | `SRC-WORLD-` |

A record marked **catalogue identified** has an identity and a planned destination. The research status separately says whether a catalogue page was inspected or bibliographic verification remains pending. Initially, no ancient book has been marked fully read. Subsequent passage dossiers add exactly inspected ranges without turning that into a full-book claim.

**Primary URL** means a checked starting resource. Its scope field states whether it is an actual work page or only a collection/register. **Planned volumes** are editorial destinations, not dates, approved plot events, or completed chapter coverage. **Caveats** retain uncertain canon membership, numbering, recensions, and source limits.

The Biblical baseline uses identities such as `SRC-BIB-GENESIS`, `SRC-BIB-1-SAMUEL`, and `SRC-BIB-SONG-OF-SONGS`. Additional works, ancient authors, later reception, and the author's legacy books remain distinct. The legacy crosswalk uses `LEGACY-CODEX-01` through `LEGACY-CODEX-30`.

# Sources behind the first creation scenes

This is the first passage dossier for *Before the Word*. It distinguishes the earlier texts from the new book's cosmology. It supports writing now while leaving voice, divine identities, and deliberate reversals to the author. The readings cover Genesis 1–3, John 1:1–18, Proverbs 8:22–31, Job 38, and one selected Coptic creation passage. They do not constitute complete readings of those five works.

The biblical translation inspected is the **New American Bible, Revised Edition (NABRE)**. Its publisher describes the edition as the revised Old Testament released in 2011 together with the 1986 New Testament. Chapter pages do not credit individual passage translators. The Coptic selection is **Bernard Barc's French translation**, hosted by Université Laval; its displayed header does not supply a revision date. These are identified modern translations, not independently collated original manuscripts. [USCCB, edition information](https://www.usccb.org/offices/new-american-bible/revised-edition-information).

## CN-01 — Genesis 1:1–31: making distinctions

Speech orders the world through separations and successive acts. Light appears before the heavenly lights, and humanity receives a shared divine image. The NABRE notes discuss the translation of *ruah* and the six-day literary pattern. A Mother existing before this speech, or a torus governing it, is a deliberate feature of our fiction. The note should identify that addition plainly. [Genesis 1, especially 1:2–5, 14–19, 26–27 and notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/genesis/1).

## CN-02 — Genesis 2:1–25: breath, work, and company

The seventh-day conclusion leads into a garden account organised around human formation, tending, prohibition, naming, and companionship. Its arrangement differs from the preceding chapter. We need to decide how the novel lets those accounts speak to each other. Lilith's presence belongs to the author's revision; this passage supplies no named Lilith. [Genesis 2:1–25; notes [2:4], [2:7], [2:9]](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/genesis/2).

## CN-03 — Genesis 3:1–24: knowledge and its consequences

The story links eating, opened eyes, shame, accusation, changed relationships, and exclusion from the life-giving tree. Its serpent is not named Satan in the passage; the NABRE note distinguishes subsequent Christian interpretation. The new book's account of refusal must show what a character knows, chooses, and risks. That moral argument is the author's work. [Genesis 3; especially 3:1–7, 16–24 and note [3:15]](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/genesis/3).

## CN-04 — John 1:1–18: the Word enters a human life

The prologue joins cosmic creation to incarnation and testimony. Its notes preserve choices about punctuation at 1:3–4, darkness at 1:5, and the reading at 1:18. Those differences should survive in the working record. Equating the Word with the Knowing Child would be a particular choice in this novel, not something established by a shared title or creation theme. [John 1:1–18, NABRE and footnotes](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John+1%3A1-18&version=NABRE).

## CN-05 — Proverbs 8:22–31: Wisdom has a voice

Wisdom describes existence before the earth and delight beside its maker and among people. The NABRE note on 8:30 records competing understandings of the word rendered as artisan. A scene can make that ambiguity consequential: different speakers may understand her as maker, companion, or child. Making her the author's Mother requires an explicit creative identification. [Proverbs 8:22–31 and note [8:30]](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/proverbs/8).

## CN-06 — Job 38:1–41: who gets to ask the questions?

The divine speech moves through construction, birth, weather, stars, and animal hunger, challenging the reach of human knowledge. The edition marks uncertainty in particular astronomical and animal terms. Our narrative may question the speaker's authority while retaining the scale of the imagery. Its measuring lines are poetic language, not supplied values for a modern equation. [Job 38 and footnotes [38:31–32], [38:36]](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Job+38&version=NABRE).

## CN-07 — A particular Coptic account: thought before speech

The inspected passage of the *Apocryphon of John* describes an invisible first principle, the manifestation of Barbelo, and an unfolding of powers in which silent thought precedes a word-linked creative act. This is one text's account. It provides a meaningful disagreement with a fiction that makes the Mother absolutely first. The novel may retain that disagreement as an attributed witness. [Bernard Barc, *Le Livre des secrets de Jean*, NH II 2,25–7,15; PDF pages 1–3](https://www.naghammadi.org/sites/naghammadi.org/files/uploads/traductions/nh-ii-1-livre-des-secrets-de-jean.pdf).

## Decisions the opening needs to make

- Establish what the narrator can know about events before ordinary time, and which claims come from later witnesses.
- Distinguish the Mother's own identity from every source figure brought into conversation with her.
- Give each changed number or physical model a declared function: literal rule of the fiction, symbolic pattern, or a character's interpretation.
- Make moral revisions change actions and consequences. A new definition of wrongdoing needs a scene that puts it under pressure.
- Label a disagreement as deliberate mystery, competing testimony, or editorial error before trying to reconcile it.

No historical date of creation is established here. The composition and manuscript dates also remain separate research questions. The first novel can carry its own convictions while the Codex explains which earlier voices it is answering.

# Lilith: where she is, and which story is speaking

Lilith is already a principal figure in this project. She has her own book in the original Codex, and Lilith “Lily” Vance is the protagonist of *The Unraveling*. The historical notes need to distinguish that established authorial role from the biblical word, the later first-wife story, and the new cosmology built around her. Those distinctions strengthen the adaptation: readers can see what it inherits, what it challenges, and what it creates.

## LN-01 — Lilith in the author's books

The Codex's Book of Lilith begins at line 888 of the parent omnibus. Its preface rejects accusations of harming children and makes refusal her defining act. Chapter One gives her the same material origin as Adam and turns their conflict into a demand for unequal power. The Mother and Lilith already have a stated relationship: the Mother makes room; Lilith defends that room. She belongs in the cycle's foundations and Garden sequence, with her later life carried forward through the other volumes. Original Codex, Lilith preface (unpublished source reference); Chapter One (unpublished source reference).

The earlier Unraveling profile supplies a contemporary person with a particular life, temperament, and abilities. She deserves scenes of her own, rather than appearing only as an explanatory symbol. That profile and the primordial character remain separately traceable even when the fiction connects them. Lily Vance's profile (unpublished source reference).

## LN-02 — Genesis does not tell the named Lilith story

The inspected creation chapters, Genesis 1–3, do not name Lilith. The human-creation account in Genesis 2 and the naming of Eve in Genesis 3 supply different material from the later first-wife narrative. Our book can place Lilith in Eden, but that is an adaptation drawing on later reception and the author's own commitments. The difference between those sources does not demonstrate that a Lilith chapter was physically removed. [Genesis 2](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/genesis/2); [Genesis 3:20](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/genesis/3).

## LN-03 — Isaiah contains a word, not the whole biography

Isaiah 34:14 does contain the Hebrew consonants **לילית**. The NABRE retains “the lilith”; the King James Version instead gives “the screech owl.” The JPS Gender-Sensitive Edition on Sefaria retains the term while noting a demonic interpretation and an alternative night-bird reading. This is a translation and identification issue inside a passage about creatures inhabiting devastation. It supplies no account of marriage to Adam, refusal, or departure from Eden. [NABRE](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Isaiah+34%3A14&version=NABRE); [KJV](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Isaiah+34%3A14&version=KJV); [Sefaria's Hebrew and JPS display](https://www.sefaria.org/Isaiah.34.14).

A reader searching an English Bible can therefore miss the familiar spelling without a verse having disappeared. Conversely, finding the spelling does not bring the medieval narrative into Isaiah. The working glossary must retain both the Hebrew term and the selected translation, with a separate entry for the novel's character.

## LN-04 — The later first-wife account

The inspected *Alphabet of Ben Sira* episode creates Lilith from earth, presents her claim to equality with Adam, and recounts her refusal and flight after pronouncing the divine name. Angels pursue her. The story then links her to danger for infants and to protective amulets. Those later elements matter: our benevolent protector deliberately changes the portrayal. Her refusal has a textual precedent here; the author's complete character is a new interpretation. [Sefaria, *Otzar Midrashim*, alternative version, segment 34](https://www.sefaria.org/Otzar_Midrashim%2C_The_Aleph_Bet_of_ben_Sira%2C_The_Alphabet_of_ben_Sira%2C_%28alternative_version%29.34).

The English text is credited to Sefaria Community Translation; its Hebrew edition label is *Otzar Midrashim, New York, 1915*. That year identifies the printed source, not the story's composition. The exact locator here is segment 34, internal item ה. We have not equated it with a particular manuscript folio or checked every recension.

## LN-05 — Medieval setting and comic framing

The Posen Library labels the *Alphabet* entry ninth century and places it among medieval satirical narratives. Its displayed excerpt concerns the precocious Ben Sira and his teacher; it is not the Lilith passage inspected above. The library also distinguishes this work from the much earlier *Wisdom of Ben Sira*. Their similar names must not collapse them into one source. Posen's date is an attributed editorial dating, not a newly established date for every version. [Posen Library, introduction and credits](https://www.posenlibrary.com/entry/alphabet-ben-sira).

That setting leaves room for serious attention to humour. A comic frame can carry cruel assumptions, pointed criticism, or both. The new novel should identify whose certainty a joke exposes and whose pain it asks the reader to dismiss. Calling an older work satirical does not settle how every sentence functions.

## LN-06 — Mother, Lilith, and the unresolved identity rule

The Codex expressly differentiates the Mother, Lilith, and the Knowing Child through holding, protecting, and illuminating. The V2 Unraveling plan also calls Lilith a Mother-aspect and describes Lily through three possible relationships to primordial Lilith: reincarnation, fragment, or vessel. These formulations need a declared relationship in the new cycle. They may describe different levels of one cosmology, or they may preserve different draft proposals. Codex's triad (unpublished source reference); V2 mythology (unpublished source reference); V2 identity proposal (unpublished source reference).

We should decide what identity means before making memories or bodily continuity depend on it. An aspect can be a distinct person; reincarnation and possession imply different experiences and consent questions. The source apparatus cannot decide those rules on the author's behalf. It can keep the alternatives visible and prevent an accidental merger.

## LN-07 — What the reader should be told

The novel's Lilith is an original adaptive character, informed by particular earlier texts and developed through the author's manuscripts. Her refusal, protective role, relationship with the Mother, and modern existence must be expressed through consequential choices. Claims that her history was erased can belong to characters or to the fiction's world. Historical commentary needs documentary evidence before making the same claim about our world.

This dossier is a bounded beginning. It does not settle all Jewish reception, inspect incantation bowls, or establish an unbroken lineage from every earlier feminine figure. It gives the writing a firm starting point: Lilith is present, her sources are named, and her differences from them remain intentional.
