# Historical notes and how to read them

These notes accompany an original novel and Codex. They explain where the source record is firm, where interpreters disagree, and where this project makes its own choices. The Mother's priority, Lilith's role, the Omnoid, the Pattern, and the revised moral vocabulary belong to the author's cosmology unless a note explicitly identifies a particular earlier text. A story may argue forcefully for its own truth while its historical apparatus remains precise about the evidence.

The initial catalogue identifies 260 records, including all 66 books in the project's biblical baseline, major additional texts, manuscript collections, and comparative source families. A record can represent a whole work, a component, a family of works, or a research queue. These are discovery and coverage records, not 260 completed readings or 260 independent scriptures. No ancient work has been marked fully read in this initial source pass.

## HN-001 — There is more than one biblical arrangement

The baseline of 66 books is an editorial tracking device. The Catholic list published by the USCCB includes Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and the two books of Maccabees alongside the other Old Testament books. Sefaria organises the Tanakh under Torah, Prophets, and Writings. Those arrangements affect reading, expectation, and interpretation; they should not disappear merely because the new novel uses a different order. Additional Orthodox and Ethiopian/Eritrean canon claims remain marked for community- and edition-specific verification. [USCCB, “Canonical Order”](https://bible.usccb.org/bible); [Sefaria, “Torah,” “Prophets,” and “Writings”](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Tanakh).

When a reader looks up a familiar name, the glossary will preserve the source's own identity and indicate the project's chosen form. Similar titles do not guarantee the same work. The catalogue therefore keeps Meqabyan apart from Maccabees, and it flags Esdras numbering for verification in the selected edition.

## HN-002 — A surviving manuscript is not a universal canon list

The Codex Sinaiticus project describes a manuscript whose surviving contents include the New Testament, parts of the Greek Old Testament, and the Epistle of Barnabas and Shepherd of Hermas. It also explains that substantial early portions are missing, and that its New Testament order differs from familiar modern arrangements. A missing leaf is not evidence of a deliberate exclusion; inclusion in one manuscript does not establish the canonical judgement of every later community. [Codex Sinaiticus, “Content,” paragraphs 1–4](https://www.codexsinaiticus.org/en/codex/content.aspx).

This distinction matters for the novel's recovered documents. A character may interpret a gap as evidence of suppression. The historical note must identify whether the real evidence is physical loss, an editorial decision, a disputed reconstruction, or simply unknown.

## HN-003 — The Dead Sea Scrolls are a collection of different kinds of evidence

The Israel Antiquities Authority separates literary compositions, ritual objects, documents, letters, and unidentified fragments. It also describes cases where a manuscript label covers multiple compositions, or where modern scholars initially grouped fragments incorrectly. Its categories are navigational aids rather than a final resolution of every scholarly dispute. [IAA, “Manuscript Types” and “Composition Types”](https://www.deadseascrolls.org.il/learn-about-the-scrolls/scrolls-content).

The catalogue consequently keeps a work separate from a physical witness. The same story can survive in more than one copy; several different texts can occupy one physical object. A fictional archive may exploit those possibilities, but the real manuscript identifiers must remain traceable.

## HN-004 — Retelling was already part of the ancient textual world

The IAA uses “parabiblical” for works that retell, expand, or embellish scriptural narratives and laws, including the Genesis Apocryphon and Jubilees. Such a text is valuable evidence for its own interpretation and setting. It does not become an omitted chapter of Genesis merely because it tells a related story. [IAA, “Non-Biblical Compositions,” paragraph labelled “Parabiblical Texts”](https://www.deadseascrolls.org.il/learn-about-the-scrolls/scrolls-content).

Our own retelling will be labelled with the same clarity: an original work that engages earlier writings. The reader should be able to find the original passage, recognise the new scene's alterations, and understand why the author made them.

## HN-005 — Nag Hammadi is not the name of one doctrine

Université Laval's table identifies individual works, codices, tractate numbers, and manuscript pages. It also separately lists the Berlin and Bruce collections. Its collection discussion distinguishes Codex Tchacos from Nag Hammadi and distinguishes its Book of Allogenes from the Nag Hammadi work called Allogenes. These are useful reminders to begin with a named text and witness before asserting a common theology. [Université Laval, treatise tables](https://www.naghammadi.org/en/translations); [“Collections gnostiques coptes,” Codex Tchacos paragraph](https://www.naghammadi.org/collections-gnostiques-coptes).

“The Gnostics believed” will therefore be replaced, wherever possible, with an attributed statement about a particular work, group, or interpretation. Barbelo, Sophia, Bythos, Sige, and the author's Mother may be placed in creative conversation; their equivalence is not assumed as a historical finding.

## HN-006 — A voice in a poem is not automatically an identified deity

The university publisher identifies *Thunder, Perfect Mind* as the second tractate in Nag Hammadi Codex VI, occupying pages 13–21, and describes the interpretive difficulty of its literary and religious setting. The novel may give its voice a particular dramatic identity. That identification must be stated as an authorial interpretation rather than the uncontested identity of the ancient speaker. [Université Laval Press, *Le Tonnerre, Intellect parfait*, description](https://www.pulaval.com/livres/le-tonnerre-intellect-parfait-nh-vi-2-bcnh-textes-no-22).

The historical apparatus will preserve the distinction between the original work, its modern translation, a scholarly reading, and any new poem or expanded scene written for this project.

## HN-007 — A translation is an identified edition, not an invisible window

The Nag Hammadi translation project names its translators and publishers and notes that its online translations can be revised. Brill's catalogue distinguishes the work from its individual manuscript versions and from editions, translations, and commentaries. These are separate textual objects. [Université Laval, “Welcome,” translation and publication paragraphs](https://www.naghammadi.org/en); [Brill, “Overview of works” and “CTS URNs”](https://scholarlyeditions.brill.com/cglo/).

Every passage used in a finished historical note will name the edition and translator, with a stable passage locator. Where a word carries several meanings, the note will explain the choice that matters to the scene. No modern translation is silently treated as the author's own prose, and source availability does not by itself settle reuse terms.

## HN-008 — Narrative time, composition, and manuscript time are different

A tale can be set in a remote past, written or reworked much later, preserved in a still later copy, and discovered centuries after that. The BCNH project distinguishes the proposed period of original composition, translation into Coptic, copying, and discovery, while also acknowledging substantial unknowns about individual works. [Université Laval, “Collections gnostiques coptes,” opening paragraphs](https://www.naghammadi.org/collections-gnostiques-coptes).

The reference timeline therefore keeps source-narrated events, historical estimates, composition/redaction ranges, manuscript dates, and the novel's revelation order on separate tracks. A prophetic vision is not automatically a calendar forecast; a character's recollection is not automatically a reliable chronology. A mystery can remain deliberately unanswered without becoming a continuity error.

## HN-009 — Historical books also have literary and theological purposes

The USCCB's introduction explicitly distinguishes the traditional label “historical” from a promise that every detail can be independently verified. It describes the particular theological interests of the historical collections and the different emphases of Chronicles. The novel should preserve those competing perspectives before choosing how to dramatise shared events. [USCCB, “The Historical Books,” Chronicles paragraph and final methodological paragraphs](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/historicalintroduction/0).

A court record, a victorious king's account, a lament, and a later retelling will not all receive the same evidentiary weight merely because they describe the same catastrophe. In the Codex, fictional speakers may disagree; in the notes, the sources and limits of the disagreement remain visible.

## HN-010 — Dates need attribution, especially where reference tables differ

The USCCB historical introduction gives 722/721 BCE for the destruction of the northern kingdom and 587 BCE for the fall of Judah. The IAA timeline gives 586 BCE for the destruction of the First Temple. The initial project timeline should retain 587/586 BCE as an explicitly attributed dating difference until a focused chronology review resolves which convention a particular note follows. [USCCB, Kings paragraph](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/historicalintroduction/0); [IAA, “First Temple Period”](https://www.deadseascrolls.org.il/learn-about-the-scrolls/historical-timeline).

The IAA also supplies useful broad anchors for Persian rule, Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63 BCE, the destruction of Jerusalem and the Second Temple in 70 CE, and the Bar Kokhba uprising in 132–135 CE. Those anchors are cited individually; the whole table is not adopted as infallible. [IAA, “Persian Period,” “Roman Period,” and “Post Second Temple Period”](https://www.deadseascrolls.org.il/learn-about-the-scrolls/historical-timeline).

## HN-011 — A text's arrangement can compress different moments

The USCCB note on Ezra 3:1–2 distinguishes the apparent early return setting from later renewed Temple work under Darius and discusses editorial arrangement. This is precisely the kind of difference a multidimensional timeline should expose rather than flatten into a single scene date. [USCCB, Ezra 3, note [3:1–2]](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/ezra/3).

The novel can rearrange scenes for dramatic reasons. Its working records will distinguish that choice from the order in a source, and the finished note will explain a consequential departure without turning every paragraph into an academic interruption.

## HN-012 — Comparative religion needs separate voices

Corpus Coranicum separately documents Qur'anic manuscripts, transmitted variant readings, contextual texts, and commentary. That structure provides a useful model: comparison should retain each source's own language, date, setting, and interpretive status. [Corpus Coranicum, “What is being produced?”](https://corpuscoranicum.de/en/about).

The global weave will not treat similar flood stories, divine mothers, serpents, ascents, or creation images as proof of one lost universal religion. Where historical influence is proposed, the note must identify the evidence and the alternative explanations. Where the connection is invented for the novel, it will be identified as such. A tradition earns its place through a consequential encounter or idea, rather than an isolated decorative name.

## HN-013 — Electronic corpora are starting points with their own limits

GRETIL describes itself as a register of standardised electronic texts contributed from sources of varying quality. Its availability supports discovery and comparison, but the underlying edition and contributor must still be checked. Oxford's ETCSL describes a selected corpus of Sumerian literary compositions, not every Mesopotamian text. [GRETIL, “Introduction”](https://gretil.sub.uni-goettingen.de/gretil.html); [Oxford ETCSL, “Introduction”](https://etcsl.orinst.ox.ac.uk/).

A reliable catalogue therefore preserves unverified rows rather than disguising them as completed scholarship. It also avoids claiming a universal canon for traditions whose textual or oral forms do not fit that model. Living oral traditions require named communities, narrators or custodians, and context-appropriate public sources.

## HN-014 — Lilith in this project

The existing author manuscripts make Lilith's refusal and equality foundational. That is an established feature of these manuscripts and an authorial commitment of the new work. This source pass has not verified a particular ancient or medieval Lilith passage, its date, or its recension. It therefore does not claim that Genesis originally contained that account, that all ancient traditions agreed with it, or that the novel reconstructs suppressed wording.

The catalogue retains separate research records for Genesis, the *Alphabet of Ben Sira*, later Jewish reception, and the author's new Lilith books. A future historical note will quote or paraphrase only after the exact earlier passage and edition have been inspected. The new novel can remain decisive about its values while making this distinction honestly.

## HN-015 — Updated mathematics and moral vocabulary

The project may deliberately revise numbers, chronology, cosmological models, metaphors, and the vocabulary of wrongdoing. Each consequential revision will keep four things visible in the editorial record: the earlier text's number or claim; the author's revised value or meaning; whether the change is literal, symbolic, or fictional; and the effect on other scenes and diagrams.

The IAA describes a prominent 364-day calendrical scheme among the scrolls. Such a scheme is evidence for a textual calendar, not a claim that the modern solar year has that length. [IAA, “Calendrical Texts”](https://www.deadseascrolls.org.il/learn-about-the-scrolls/scrolls-content). Similarly, a torus or equation in the author's cosmology can govern the fiction without being presented as an experimentally established account of our universe.

These distinctions leave room for humour, allegory, and conviction. They give readers a way to tell what the source says, what an interpreter proposes, and what this book creates.

# Chronology: story, history and experience

This is a populated planning chronology for all twelve volumes. All event selections, synthetic consequences and first-safe chapters are **editorial proposals**. Each row is an anchor awaiting full scene development, not a claim that a chapter is complete.

Source-story order is not a calibrated universal timeline. Historical dates remain unknown unless a bounded source supports them. Realm and personal elapsed times remain explicitly unestablished. Composition dates are separate: an exile setting does not date the writing of Daniel.

The historical date discrepancy **587/586 BCE** is preserved. The 538 return tradition and 520 rebuilding resumption are distinct events and not an eighteen-year transit. Date ranges in the data identify whether they are duration, disagreement, context or a grouping of different events.

## Volume 01: Before the Word

Creation and separation; no historical date established.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-001 · The Mother as possibility | Codex: Book of the Mother | Unestablished | V01-C01 | The frame has not yet produced a shared calendar. |
| EV-002 · The First Flame experiences loneliness | V2: Core Mythology | Unestablished | V01-C03 | A need for company becomes a creative motive, not automatic justification. |
| EV-003 · Creation as relation | Codex: Mother and Father | Unestablished | V01-C05 | Neither source nor recipient owns every being that follows. |
| EV-004 · The divine children emerge | V2: Firstborn | Unestablished | V01-C07 | Kinship begins before agreed limits and institutions. |
| EV-005 · The claim to precedence | Codex: first wound | Unestablished | V01-C09 | Authority begins to cite age as entitlement. |
| EV-006 · Separation interrupts relation | Codex: Mother / Torus | Unestablished | V01-C11 | Loss produces a debt of repair that later radiance cannot cancel. |

## Volume 02: The Garden and the Refusal

Garden, naming, knowledge, exile, first families.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-007 · Naming in the Garden | Genesis 2; Codex: Adam | Unestablished | V02-C01 | Naming becomes useful and dangerous when confused with ownership. |
| EV-008 · Lilith refuses subordination | Codex: Lilith; later Lilith tradition requires source note | Unestablished | V02-C03 | Departure preserves refusal while imposing material costs. |
| EV-009 · Eve enters an inherited arrangement | Genesis 2; two Codex Eve variants | Unestablished | V02-C05 | Created conditions are not equivalent to chosen conditions. |
| EV-010 · The fruit and disputed knowledge | Genesis 3; Codex: Knowing Child | Unestablished | V02-C07 | Knowledge creates responsibility without guaranteeing wisdom. |
| EV-011 · Departure and changed embodiment | Genesis 3 | Unestablished | V02-C09 | World and personal consequences continue after the gate closes. |
| EV-012 · Abel’s death and Cain’s mark | Genesis 4 | Unestablished | V02-C11 | Protection from retaliation is not cancellation of harm. |

## Volume 03: The Waters and the Scattering

Watchers, flood traditions, Babel and migrations.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-013 · The Watchers cross a boundary | 1 Enoch 6–16; Genesis 6 comparison | Unestablished | V03-C01 | Instruction, desire and power are judged by what they do to others. |
| EV-014 · Enoch receives conflicting measures | 1 Enoch: journeys and luminaries | Unestablished | V03-C03 | A traveller’s report does not synchronize all clocks. |
| EV-015 · Warning and preparation | Genesis 6 | Unestablished | V03-C05 | Knowledge is unevenly distributed before catastrophe. |
| EV-016 · The flood and its witnesses | Genesis 7–8; flood parallels kept separate | Unestablished | V03-C07 | Survival accounts cannot recover every lost perspective. |
| EV-017 · Covenant after devastation | Genesis 9 | Unestablished | V03-C09 | An oath after disaster leaves grief, hunger and accountability. |
| EV-018 · Babel and scattering | Genesis 11 | Unestablished | V03-C11 | Shared language, coercive unity and migration remain distinguishable. |

## Volume 04: The Houses of Covenant

Ancestral households and Joseph; dates unestablished.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-019 · Abram’s departure | Genesis 12 | Unestablished | V04-C01 | A promised future changes the lives of people who did not receive the promise. |
| EV-020 · Hagar is sent away and seen | Genesis 16; 21 as distinct later departure | Unestablished | V04-C03 | Household survival does not justify making someone expendable. |
| EV-021 · Hospitality and the destroyed cities | Genesis 18–19 | Unestablished | V04-C05 | The fate of bystanders complicates every claim of collective guilt. |
| EV-022 · The binding and its aftermath | Genesis 22; reception variants separate | Unestablished | V04-C07 | A halted act can leave lasting fear and broken trust. |
| EV-023 · Jacob wrestles with inheritance | Genesis 25–36 | Unestablished | V04-C09 | A changed name does not pay every old debt. |
| EV-024 · Joseph, grain and reconciliation | Genesis 37–50 | Unestablished | V04-C11 | Power over food can rescue and subordinate at the same time. |

## Volume 05: Bondage and Liberation

Egypt, departure, wilderness, law and revolt.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-025 · An empire organizes bondage | Exodus 1–2 | Unestablished | V05-C01 | Labour, households and official language conceal unequal vulnerability. |
| EV-026 · A name at the burning bush | Exodus 3–4 | Unestablished | V05-C03 | A voice’s authority and its referent are recorded separately. |
| EV-027 · Plagues and contested warning | Exodus 7–12 | Unestablished | V05-C05 | The narrative retains civilian suffering and competing testimony. |
| EV-028 · Departure and the crossing | Exodus 12–15 | Unestablished | V05-C07 | A disputed route is never drawn as a surveyed itinerary. |
| EV-029 · Law, food and worship | Exodus 16–34; Leviticus | Unestablished | V05-C09 | Daily provision and legal authority bind different obligations. |
| EV-030 · Revolt and the generation’s end | Numbers; Deuteronomy 34 | Unestablished | V05-C11 | Liberation does not guarantee that the new community remains just. |

## Volume 06: The Land and the Crowns

Settlement traditions, judges and monarchy.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-031 · Entry and contested land | Joshua | Unestablished | V06-C01 | Conquest traditions are narrated alongside the losses of inhabitants. |
| EV-032 · Judges, cycles and local survival | Judges | Unestablished | V06-C03 | Repeated violence changes the ground; the cycle is not a reset. |
| EV-033 · Ruth and the work of belonging | Ruth | Unestablished | V06-C05 | Kinship decisions arise inside economic precarity. |
| EV-034 · The demand for a king | 1 Samuel 8–15 | Unestablished | V06-C07 | A collective demand gives rulers power without ending accountability. |
| EV-035 · David, Bathsheba and royal harm | 2 Samuel 11–12 | Unestablished | V06-C09 | Public achievement cannot redeem an exploitation by accounting trick. |
| EV-036 · Solomon builds and extracts | 1 Kings 1–11 | Unestablished | V06-C11 | Temple, wealth and labour are held in the same frame. |

## Volume 07: The Kingdoms and the Exile

Divided kingdoms, imperial conquest and exile.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-037 · A kingdom divides | 1 Kings 12 | Unestablished | V07-C01 | Inherited extraction creates lasting political fracture. |
| EV-038 · Prophets contest wealth and worship | Amos; Hosea; Isaiah; prophetic corpus | Unestablished | V07-C03 | Prophetic testimony remains situated and sometimes contested. |
| EV-039 · Samaria falls | 2 Kings 17; institutional chronology | 722/721 BCE | V07-C05 | Displacement changes language, land and household continuity. |
| EV-040 · Jerusalem is destroyed and people displaced | 2 Kings 25; Jeremiah; Lamentations | 587/586 BCE | V07-C07 | 587/586 BCE is retained as a source discrepancy, not averaged. |
| EV-041 · Lament and vision in exile | Ezekiel; exile traditions; Daniel narrative setting | Unestablished | V07-C09 | The time represented in a book is not its composition date. |
| EV-042 · Babylon passes to Persian rule | Institutional historical anchor; Ezra context | 539 BCE | V07-C11 | A changed imperial policy opens possibilities without instant restoration. |

## Volume 08: The Return and the Hidden Years

Persian return, diaspora and Hellenistic resistance.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-043 · Return is permitted and uneven | Ezra 1–3; historical note at Ezra 3:1–2 | 538 return tradition; 520 rebuilding resumption | V08-C01 | Departure from exile and rebuilding have separate dates and participants. |
| EV-044 · Rebuilding and contested belonging | Ezra; Nehemiah; Haggai | Unestablished | V08-C03 | Restoration can create new exclusions and old grievances. |
| EV-045 · Diaspora lives: Esther and Tobit | Esther; Tobit; their narrative settings kept distinct | Unestablished | V08-C05 | Different diaspora stories do not become a single dated episode. |
| EV-046 · Judith’s resistance and historical tension | Judith | Unestablished | V08-C07 | Deliberate literary dislocations are recorded, not silently repaired. |
| EV-047 · Maccabean resistance and its costs | 1–2 Maccabees; Hellenistic context | Second century BCE context only | V08-C09 | Resistance can gain authority while losing the innocence it claims. |
| EV-048 · Rome enters the regional balance | 63 BCE Pompey anchor; pre-Gospel setting | 63 BCE | V08-C11 | The political field inherited by Gospel characters is assembled before them. |

## Volume 09: The Word in Flesh

Jesus and contemporaries; distinct Gospel witnesses.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-049 · Birth accounts and their different clocks | Matthew 1–2; Luke 1–2 | Unestablished | V09-C01 | The witnesses’ settings are retained without invented exact harmonization. |
| EV-050 · Baptism and the wilderness | Mark 1; Matthew 3–4; Luke 3–4; John 1 | Unestablished | V09-C03 | A public claim and a private ordeal establish different evidence. |
| EV-051 · Meals, teaching and the excluded | Gospel teaching and encounter cycles | Unestablished | V09-C05 | Care changes immediate material relations as well as belief. |
| EV-052 · Jerusalem and the contest over authority | Gospel Jerusalem cycles | Unestablished | V09-C07 | Crowds, officials and friends carry incompatible expectations. |
| EV-053 · Arrest, execution and abandonment | Distinct Passion narratives | Unestablished | V09-C09 | Death and political violence are not made painless by later meaning. |
| EV-054 · Resurrection testimony and changed obligations | Distinct resurrection witnesses | Unestablished | V09-C11 | A return does not erase what mourners, witnesses and betrayers experienced. |

## Volume 10: The Witnesses and the Empires

Communities, letters, journeys and disputed authority.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-055 · Pentecost and public witness | Acts 1–2 | Unestablished | V10-C01 | Shared speech does not require identical experience. |
| EV-056 · Scarcity and distribution | Acts 4–6; community traditions | Unestablished | V10-C03 | Belief meets the bookkeeping of food and care. |
| EV-057 · Paul’s changed allegiance | Acts 9; Galatians 1; accounts kept distinct | Unestablished | V10-C05 | Changed commitment does not undo earlier harm. |
| EV-058 · Belonging disputed across communities | Acts 15; Galatians; community letters | Unestablished | V10-C07 | A council scene cannot settle every community’s later argument. |
| EV-059 · Letters, journeys and unequal authority | Acts journey sequences; Pauline corpus | Unestablished | V10-C09 | Delivery dates, composition dates and narrated journeys remain separate. |
| EV-060 · Jerusalem’s Temple is destroyed | 70 CE historical anchor; later reception | 70 CE | V10-C11 | Collective catastrophe transforms interpretation without supplying a universal verdict. |

## Volume 11: The Unveilings and the Inheritances

Apocalyptic testimony and later transmission.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-061 · A visionary writes from Patmos | Revelation narrative frame | Unestablished | V11-C01 | Vision order, depicted event order and writing date are separate tracks. |
| EV-062 · Unveilings circulate as competing hopes | Revelation; apocalyptic traditions with independent entries | Unestablished | V11-C03 | An image can promise release to one community and terrify another. |
| EV-063 · A later revolt changes the landscape | 132–135 CE institutional historical anchor | 132–135 CE | V11-C05 | A historical event is not automatically a fulfilment of a prophecy. |
| EV-064 · Books travel, change and survive | Source-specific manuscript transmission histories | Unestablished | V11-C07 | Copying, translation, loss and canon selection require separate evidence. |
| EV-065 · Traditions intersect without becoming identical | World-religion source braids; individual traditions independently sourced | Unestablished | V11-C09 | A fictional underlying relation must not masquerade as historical proof. |
| EV-066 · Institutions inherit both care and harm | Later reception; source-by-source research | Unestablished | V11-C11 | No institution is made timeless, uniform or exempt from internal dissent. |

## Volume 12: The Return of Names

Modern remembering, selected Unraveling and aftermath.

| Event | Source-story anchor | Historical date | Proposed first-safe chapter | Lasting consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EV-067 · Lily dies and the world continues | Original Unraveling prologue; V2 alternative | Unestablished | V12-C01 | Do not import an old exact death interval until this version adopts it. |
| EV-068 · Remembering meets a living biography | V2 awakening and incarnation premise | Unestablished | V12-C03 | A recovered identity cannot displace the present person’s consent. |
| EV-069 · Names, dice and allies become consequential | V2 HALO and supporting cast | Unestablished | V12-C05 | Twenty-four symbols open 512 ordered combinations, not unlimited control. |
| EV-070 · The Architect’s claim is tested | Original Architect history versus V2 Eve identity | Unestablished | V12-C13 | Evidence must settle an occupant claim before the story treats it as settled. |
| EV-071 · The lost are approached on their terms | Codex lost domains; V2 recovery candidates | Unestablished | V12-C09 | Restoration asks who lived through the interval and what they now want. |
| EV-072 · Return of names and unfinished repair | Approved finale direction; new scene work required | Unestablished | V12-C11 | Victory changes who can choose; grief and obligations remain. |

## Historical references

The northern fall is recorded as 722/721 BCE in the [USCCB historical introduction](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/historicalintroduction/0). The same introduction gives 587 BCE for Judah; the [Israel Antiquities Authority timeline](https://www.deadseascrolls.org.il/learn-about-the-scrolls/historical-timeline) uses 586 BCE. These sources are not silently averaged.

The [Metropolitan Museum’s Cyrus Cylinder exhibition](https://www.metmuseum.org/exhibitions/listings/2013/cyrus-cylinder) supports Cyrus’s capture of Babylon in 539 BCE and explicitly notes that the cylinder does not name the Jews. The [note at Ezra 3:1–2](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/ezra/3) distinguishes an apparent 538 return from building resuming in 520.

The [IAA timeline](https://www.deadseascrolls.org.il/learn-about-the-scrolls/historical-timeline) supplies the bounded 63 BCE, 70 CE and 132–135 CE anchors used here. Its other dates have not been imported wholesale.

## Many-clock contract

Every drafted journey or return must record departure and arrival witnesses, source and destination realm, world elapsed time, personal elapsed time, conversion rule if known, and a changed condition that remains afterward. If a duration is not established, write unknown. Never substitute zero or assume a 1:1 rate.

Example only: a character experiences six hours while seventy-two world hours pass under an adopted constant 1:12 rate. People outside have lived three days. A missed burial, an expired promise or a changed government is still real when the traveller returns. This arithmetic example is not canon for any realm.

# Creation-sequence continuity packet

This packet supports Volume I and its bridge into Eden. The approved directions are the Omnoid frame; distinct source, aspect, manifestation and incarnation identities; agency and responsibility; and multiple clocks with lasting consequences. The detailed sequence below is an **editorial proposal**. An older manuscript establishes that a claim exists in the source material, not that the author has adopted it or that it is externally established physics.

Latest author steering selects C’s panoramic, irreverent narration with more natural camaraderie. That voice choice does not silently ratify every gate mechanism or cosmological identity in a calibration scene.

“Material effect” means a change a scene can make perceptible: warmth, an unanswered address, a missing presence, a failed provision or a changed relationship. It does not require matter, bodies or measured seconds to exist before their introduction. Proposed first-safe chapters indicate disclosure limits, not historical dates.

## 1. The Mother before an answer — V01-C01

**Source:** “Before the Light, there was the Mother.” [S1] Her later recollection also says “Not lonely.” [S2]

**Observer and knowledge:** Mother may experience holding and the absence of an independent answer. A later Mother recounting this to Lilith is retrospective testimony, not the same narrative position as Mother experiencing it initially.

**Effect and capability:** The draft can make an invitation remain unanswered. Holding space is inherited vocabulary; deliberately leaving an interval unfilled is a new proposed limit. Its cost is unresolved expectation, not an invented loss of energy.

**Consequence and uncertainty:** Once another answer becomes possible, its independence cannot be withdrawn merely to guarantee agreement. Wanting an answer need not mean loneliness. Whether Mother already knows every possible response remains undecided.

**Disclosure:** Introduce a limited encounter before explaining the complete cosmology.

**Catchable failures:** Mother is called lonely as settled canon; a narrator supplies measured seconds before any clock; silence is treated as another being’s consent.

## 2. The First Flame wakes — V01-C02

**Source:** The Father’s account says, “I didn't know the Mother was there.” [S3] V2 calls First Flame the original consciousness. [S4]

**Observer and knowledge:** A close First Flame viewpoint can know its own fear, longing and expression, while misreading surrounding support as absence. It cannot immediately know the Mother’s identity if the nonrecognition strand is retained.

**Effect and capability:** Light or warmth makes the first perceptible contrast. Concentrating expression into an inhabitable encounter is a proposed capability limit. The cost is restraint and uncertainty, not a quantified cosmological fuel budget.

**Consequence and uncertainty:** Expression changes what another can encounter. Father and First Flame remain a proposed aspect relationship; “first” may describe this speaker’s experience rather than absolute ontological priority.

**Disclosure:** Name the experienced contrast; withhold a universal explanation of its mechanics.

**Catchable failures:** First Flame recognizes Mother without a recognition event; “original consciousness” silently erases her prior awareness; restraint is presented as an existing source equation.

## 3. The first distinction becomes a relationship — V01-C03

**Source:** Mother remembers a presence “somehow separate from my own” while also describing it as always part of her. [S2]

**Observer and knowledge:** Each participant may recognize a response it did not dictate. Neither gains unrestricted access to the other’s intentions merely through shared origin.

**Effect and capability:** An address, refusal or unanswered question changes the relationship. Making a place neither controls alone is a proposed dramatization. Its cost is lost unilateral control; its capability is coordinated action without identity merger.

**Consequence and uncertainty:** An independent response cannot become retroactively predetermined simply because the relationship later coheres. Separate identity, an aspect becoming perceptible and retrospective language about an earlier unity remain different possibilities.

**Disclosure:** Show a practicable refusal before declaring the agreement voluntary.

**Catchable failures:** “Part of me” becomes ownership; both speakers know each other’s private thoughts without a mechanism; the first disagreement is cured by merging their identities.

## 4. Divine children and unequal needs — V01-C04–C07

**Source:** The Father describes making companions; later commentary calls Firstborn “fixed, complete, perfect mirrors.” [S5] Mother nevertheless expects children to learn and grow. [S6]

**Observer and knowledge:** A child knows its own need or refusal. A parent’s classification of that child is fallible. A proposed recorder can report appearances and testimony, not acquire omniscience by keeping a ledger.

**Effect and capability:** A refused office, unsuitable provision or missed appointment exposes difference. Distinct needs and negotiated clocks are proposed scene mechanisms. Care costs attention, revision and relinquished expectations.

**Consequence and uncertainty:** A child’s refusal leaves a real vacancy; later acceptance does not erase the earlier refusal. Whether Firstborn can change is unresolved, so neither immutable programming nor effortless growth may enter unnoticed.

**Disclosure:** Establish one child’s limits before extrapolating to the whole class.

**Catchable failures:** Every Firstborn shares one motive; a recorder knows an unspoken intention; the text promises growth while also asserting absolute changelessness.

## 5. Misrecognition becomes an order — V01-C08–C10

**Source:** The First Wound sequence says the Firstborn could not perceive Mother and declared war on darkness. [S7]

**Observer and knowledge:** Show who mistakes nonperception for nonexistence, who endorses that inference and who receives the order. Distinguish an institutional record from the event it describes.

**Effect and capability:** A restriction closes an available path or makes care inaccessible. The precise office, decree and enforcement mechanism are new proposals. Their cost falls on named recipients, not only on the ruler’s conscience.

**Consequence and uncertainty:** An order can produce harm before its author understands it. Mere access to source power does not grant the capacity to know everything. The individual Firstborn involved, including Lucifer’s position, require decisions rather than inherited collective guilt.

**Disclosure:** Readers need enough evidence to see the mistake without receiving a catalogue of all divine motives.

**Catchable failures:** Darkness itself becomes evil; a divine title proves an order legitimate; a protective office’s good intentions cancel the injured person’s loss.

## 6. Separation, withdrawal and the missing place — V01-C11–C12

**Source:** Mother “withdrew” after the First Wound; the Hollow is described there as grief after her loss. [S7] The Father later confesses his own avoidance. [S8]

**Observer and knowledge:** Those remaining can observe a failed reply or changed condition. They cannot certify the absent being’s destruction, destination or private intention from absence alone.

**Effect and capability:** Withdrawal changes access and provision. Opening a usable departure threshold is a separate proposed action, not automatically the same event as coerced retreat. The cost is separation and the labour of maintaining or losing relation.

**Consequence and uncertainty:** The interval lived apart remains real after reunion. Mother’s retreat, children departing and Father withdrawing are three distinguishable events. The Hollow’s nature and precise onset remain disputed across drafts. Mother’s proposed “enduring loneliness” conflicts with her earlier “Not lonely” and needs explicit selection or an actual change in her experience.

**Disclosure:** Withhold the missing person’s fate until a witness or encounter supports it.

**Catchable failures:** Voluntary departure substitutes for attack without acknowledging the change; absence proves death; reunion resets the elapsed world; grief is equated with moral corruption.

## 7. The bridge into Eden — V02-C01 onward

**Source:** The Father’s account makes the garden a place “where things could become rather than simply be.” [S9] It also says “Adam first” and “created at the same moment” within one verse. [S9]

**Observer and knowledge:** A garden witness can encounter soil, bodies and rules without knowing the entire creation history. Later testimony may connect these experiences to earlier beings without resolving every identity at once.

**Effect and capability:** Embodiment makes hunger, injury, shelter and distance consequential. Garden provision is inherited in broad form; name-surrender procedures and a bell costing an outside hour belong to current calibration inventions. [S10]

**Consequence and uncertainty:** A new home does not erase preceding conflict. Human origin as clay, called-forth new flames or a returning identity must not be equated without adoption. Adam/Lilith simultaneity and sequence remain an explicit source tension.

**Disclosure:** Introduce the Garden’s operative conditions before their explanatory genealogy. Preserve Genesis and later Lilith reception as distinct sources.

**Catchable failures:** A pin on Earth is declared Eden’s verified location; the calibration bell becomes a universal realm rate; human creation silently proves Father/Mother/Lilith identity; later Lilith tradition is attributed directly to Genesis.

## First-chapter review gate

The chapter should let a reader identify an experienced want, a response that cannot simply be commanded and a changed condition by the end. It need not settle the Omnoid’s exact geometry, Mother’s complete knowledge or the Father/First Flame equivalence. Humour should arise from a speaker’s limited grasp or failed expectation; an injured being’s suffering need not be discharged by a joke. Distinguish retrospective knowledge from present perception wherever narration crosses between them.

A review should cite the failing sentence and the rule it silently decided. Structural validity is not author approval. The accompanying packet records stage dependencies, source evidence and review examples; its proposed chronology is not permission to overwrite older variants.

## Where Lilith belongs

Lilith is a person in her own account, not a collective label for women. Her Codex preface says, “The Mother holds. I PROTECT what she holds,” and describes them as partners. [S13] The Father’s account locates her embodied arrival beside Adam in the Garden. [S9] V2 instead offers Mother-aspect language and later leaves “reincarnation/fragment/vessel” as alternatives. None of this establishes that Lilith was absent from every pre-Garden domain, or authorizes identifying her with Mother.

For the first chapter, distinguish **embodied chronological entry** from **a later framing witness**. The existing Mother narrative addresses a later Lilith while remembering creation. A panoramic telling can preserve that structure, but must signal its vantage rather than silently inserting Garden-era Lilith into the first moment. Whether to use that frame is an editorial choice; her ontology remains a separate decision.

## Source locations and authority

S1–S3 and S5–S9 refer to ILLUMINATED_CODEX_COMPLETE.md (unpublished source reference): S1 lines 43–65; S2 185–205; S3 4625–4637; S5 4681–4719; S6 221–225; S7 421–457; S8 4525–4547; S9 4685–4707. These are literary witnesses with unconfirmed author adoption.

S4 is V2 (unpublished source reference), lines 21–49. Its attribution “From your notes” has not been traced here to a direct author statement. S10 is [the calibration treatments](/codex-apockalypsis/library/calibration-voice-samples); the original opening labels the treatments unadopted, while the latest steering now selects C’s voice. S13 is Lilith’s preface (unpublished source reference), lines 916–922. The source catalogue identifies Genesis but marks full-text inspection false; this packet does not upgrade that research status.

# World reference and identity guide

This reference supports all twelve novels and their complete parallel Codex. The Omnoid frame, distinct source/aspect/incarnation identities, agency-based ethics and lasting consequences across different clocks are approved directions. Detailed names, reconciliations and mechanics below are **editorial proposals**, including material inherited from older drafts. Their presence does not mean the author has adopted every claim.

## How the cosmology fits together

The Omnoid is the larger frame. Historical Earth and the proposed realms are local settings or experiences within that frame, rather than a ladder of increasingly worthy people. A journey may change how somebody can take form without making that person a new owner’s property. Returning to life or remembering a former life does not restore a world that waited unchanged.

The older material contains three incompatible numbered systems. We preserve them by distinguishing **realm geography**, **gate functions**, and **cultivation vocabularies**. The Threshold can be a place and a similarly named operation without being the sixth realm merely because a gate table lists it sixth. Crown can be a realm name and a stage label without making the two interchangeable. This separation is a proposed reconciliation, not a claim about the author’s unstated intention.

The Mother and Lilith remain distinguishable. One may express an aspect of the other while retaining an independent biography, agency and right to refuse. The Father is a candidate aspect of the First Flame. Lucifer’s light is not automatically identical to the source flame. Mary’s motherhood does not establish identity with the Mother. The Architect is indexed as a role because the original and V2 disagree about who occupies it.

## Darkness, power and responsibility

These ethical principles do not make the fictional world harmless. Characters and institutions can coerce, exploit, misinterpret, kill and refuse repair. The story follows the effects on people and places. It does not make power, antiquity, divine rank or narrative importance an exemption from responsibility. Nor does it require injured people to forgive so that a protagonist’s arc can feel complete.

Repair requires changed conditions. Restitution, food, shelter, changed institutions, restored choices and sustained care can matter more than a speech. A return or a recovered name leaves other people’s grief and decisions intact. Humour can expose divine bureaucracy, status anxiety and self-importance while leaving the suffering beneath them real.

## What the mathematics establishes

Three distinguished eight-sided dice provide twenty-four named faces and **512 ordered combinations**. Equal chances require the additional assumptions that the dice are fair and independent; those assumptions have not been adopted as the actual magical rules. The formal check verifies the arithmetic, not divination.

The Omnoid and Wolfspace source papers contain unresolved mathematical language. A picture of a torus is not proof of a physical theory. The internal notes preserve the source conflicts and use only bounded, explicit arithmetic models for elapsed time. They make no claim that fictional travel, consciousness or afterlife mechanisms are established science.

## Navigation and spoiler policy

The identity index is a writer-facing reference. Its first-safe chapter values are proposed reveal positions that must be reconciled with the narrative outline. A reader edition should filter facts by the chapter reached. This complete reference intentionally exposes later candidates so the writing team can detect contradictions.

The editable atlas preserves named relations, broad locations and sequence. It loses true distance between realms, exact historical roads and any universal rate between clocks. Its map legends state these limits directly.



## Realms

| Realm | Role | Clock | Cost or failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Omnoid | A containing relation, not an extra numbered biome. | Unknown; no global clock has been established. | No map can make every history simultaneously readable. |
| Earth / historical world | The biblical and historical spine, with geographic and cultural specificity. | Historical dating when supported; otherwise relative story order. | Distance, institutions, bodies and material scarcity matter. |
| Fundament | Baseline embodied experience in the Unraveling vocabulary. | Local rate unknown. | Ordinary vulnerability persists even when other realms are perceived. |
| Threshold | Traversable liminality; places become accessible under stated local conditions. | Rate and transit duration must be set scene by scene. | Disorientation, missed appointments and incompatible passage terms. |
| Labyrinth | Paths and alternatives may be encountered without deleting enacted history. | Sequence is known only along a traveller’s own route. | Confusing a possible self with the person who owes a present obligation. |
| Reflection | Encounter with contested self-image and other witnesses. | No universal conversion to Earth time. | Insight may be partial; reflected agreement is not consent. |
| Engine | Experience of local reality’s mechanisms. | Causal processes need declared before/after ordering. | Intervention has system-wide costs; explanatory access is not unlimited power. |
| Web | Connections and their histories made navigable. | Concurrent contacts may have different experienced durations. | Connection can burden, expose or betray; participation is revocable. |
| Sight | Perception and interpretation become terrain. | Observation order differs from event order. | Seeing one view does not settle all testimony. |
| Crown | A high-order meeting with the limits of an individual perspective. | Access duration unestablished. | Scale can obscure individual suffering; no moral rank is granted. |
| Eden | The Garden of the selected narrative; its Earth coordinates are unestablished. | Source sequence only. | Leaving changes relationships and conditions; no easy return erases exile. |
| Lost domains | Four missing domains in older drafts; loss, hiddenness and inaccessibility are distinct possibilities. | Unknown. | Do not import recovered realms without accounting for inhabitants and elapsed time. |
| Gyre / Eight Reaches | Sevenfold Theft topology, provisionally held beside the biblical series. | Its chronology is uncorrelated with Earth. | No crossover is established solely by a torus, a Threshold or seven Thrones. |
| Wolfspace pockets | Folded-access motif in the Sevenfold companion paper. | Unknown; its equations do not supply a validated conversion. | Pocket accessibility and costs require a future adopted rule. |


## Identity index

| ID | Name and kind | Distinction to preserve | First-safe chapter |
|---|---|---|---|
| E-OMNOID | **Omnoid** — frame | The encompassing cosmological frame; not an actor merely because it contains actors. | V01-C01 |
| E-MOTHER | **The Mother** — source candidate | Primordial receptive depth in the Codex; distinguish from every daughter or local title. | V01-C01 |
| E-FIRST-FLAME | **First Flame** — source candidate | Lonely creative consciousness in the existing drafts; Father-aspect is not the whole source. | V01-C01 |
| E-FATHER | **The Father** — aspect candidate | A relational creative aspect; a command attributed to Father still requires speaker and witness. | V01-C01 |
| E-LILITH | **Lilith** — incarnation lineage candidate | A distinct sovereign identity expressing refusal and equality; Mother-aspect resemblance does not erase her biography. | V02-C01 |
| E-ADAM | **Adam** — mortal lineage candidate | Naming, blame and the difficult practice of repair; no forgiveness is owed automatically. | V02-C01 |
| E-EVE | **Eve** — mortal lineage candidate | Knowledge and choice under inherited coercion; two substantial draft versions remain preserved. | V02-C01 |
| E-SOPHIA | **Sophia / the Knowing Child** — aspect candidate | The Codex gives this figure the serpent and awakening roles; comparative traditions remain independently sourced. | V02-C01 |
| E-SERPENT | **The Garden Serpent** — manifestation candidate | A narrative manifestation linked to Sophia in one draft; not a universal identity claim. | V02-C01 |
| E-LUCIFER | **Lucifer / Lightbringer** — aspect candidate | Illumination and dissent; Firstborn provenance does not make Light identical to First Flame. | V01-C01 |
| E-CAIN | **Cain** — source tradition character | Fratricide, protection and displacement; violence survives the perpetrator’s explanation. | V02-C01 |
| E-ABEL | **Abel** — source tradition character | A person with a life before becoming evidence in another person’s moral argument. | V02-C01 |
| E-ENOCH | **Enoch** — source tradition character | Journeying witness whose experience and transmitted books are different clocks. | V03-C01 |
| E-NOAH | **Noah** — source tradition character | Survival, covenant and the unequal aftermath of catastrophe. | V03-C01 |
| E-ABRAHAM | **Abraham** — source tradition character | A covenant household leader whose hospitality and coercive decisions both have consequences. | V04-C01 |
| E-SARAH | **Sarah** — source tradition character | Covenant participant with desires and power beyond an heir-producing function. | V04-C01 |
| E-HAGAR | **Hagar** — source tradition character | Expulsion and survival seen from the person made expendable by a household. | V04-C01 |
| E-ISHMAEL | **Ishmael** — source tradition character | A lineage-bearing person; do not reduce him to a comparative-religion connector. | V04-C01 |
| E-ISAAC | **Isaac** — source tradition character | Inheritance shaped by the remembered threat of sacrifice. | V04-C01 |
| E-JACOB | **Jacob / Israel** — source tradition character | Naming, rivalry, exile and changed obligations. | V04-C01 |
| E-JOSEPH | **Joseph** — source tradition character | Trafficking survivor who later controls grain, access and dependence. | V04-C01 |
| E-MOSES | **Moses** — source tradition character | Liberator and lawgiver; claims to authority remain accountable to the governed. | V05-C01 |
| E-MIRIAM | **Miriam** — source tradition character | Leadership, song, challenge and communal memory. | V05-C01 |
| E-AARON | **Aaron** — source tradition character | Ritual leadership operating under divided pressures. | V05-C01 |
| E-JOSHUA | **Joshua** — source tradition character | Conquest testimony must retain the lives and claims of inhabitants. | V06-C01 |
| E-RUTH | **Ruth** — source tradition character | Migration, labour, kinship and consent within material insecurity. | V06-C01 |
| E-SAMUEL | **Samuel** — source tradition character | Prophetic authority and the demand for a king. | V06-C01 |
| E-SAUL | **Saul** — source tradition character | Kingship’s insecurity and the machinery of belonging. | V06-C01 |
| E-DAVID | **David** — source tradition character | A ruler whose poetry and charisma do not cancel exploitation. | V06-C01 |
| E-BATHSHEBA | **Bathsheba** — source tradition character | Political and personal survival; retain perspective beyond royal desire. | V06-C01 |
| E-SOLOMON | **Solomon** — source tradition character | Wisdom and centralization; distinguish this lineage from V2 Threshold-dweller Solomon. | V06-C01 |
| E-ESTHER | **Esther** — source tradition character | Diaspora survival amid royal violence; narrative setting is not a secure event date. | V08-C01 |
| E-JUDITH | **Judith** — source tradition character | Resistance narrative with deliberate historical tensions; no false imperial harmonization. | V08-C01 |
| E-TOBIT | **Tobit** — source tradition character | Diaspora, care, burial and restored relationships; narrated era differs from transmission. | V08-C01 |
| E-JESUS | **Jesus** — incarnation identity under review | Incarnational identity is central to the selected narrative; preserve distinct testimony before choosing fictional synthesis. | V09-C01 |
| E-MARY | **Mary, mother of Jesus** — source tradition character | Embodied family and witness; no automatic identity with the primordial Mother. | V09-C01 |
| E-MAGDALENE | **Mary Magdalene** — source tradition character | A witness with agency; distinguish named women and avoid conflated biographies. | V09-C01 |
| E-PETER | **Peter** — source tradition character | Devotion, failure and competing claims of leadership. | V09-C01 |
| E-PAUL | **Paul** — source tradition character | Letters address situated communities; do not turn all disputed reception into a single speaker. | V10-C01 |
| E-JOHN-PATMOS | **John of Patmos** — witness identity under review | The visionary named in Revelation; do not automatically equate with every Johannine author. | V11-C01 |
| E-LILY | **Lily / Lilith Vance** — incarnation candidate | Modern Unraveling identity; remembering cannot erase her present relationships or replace her consent. | V12-C01 |
| E-JUNE | **June Park** — existing draft character | Probability-sensitive ally whose loyalty must remain a choice. | V12-C01 |
| E-YUNA | **Yuna** — existing draft character | A child witness; exceptional perception does not justify adults instrumentalizing her. | V12-C01 |
| E-ARCHITECT | **The Architect** — role with competing occupants | Former Keeper in the original; Eve in V2. Role and occupant are separately indexed. | V12-C01 |
| E-THRESHOLD-SOLOMON | **Solomon of the Threshold** — existing draft character | V2 toll-keeper; no confirmed equivalence to the ancient king. | V12-C01 |
| E-HOLLOW | **The Hollow** — condition or actor under review | Drafts alternate entropy, loneliness and wounded relation; avoid diagnosing actual people through this metaphor. | V03-C01 |
| E-CAEL | **Cael Morrow** — adjacent continuity candidate | Sevenfold Theft protagonist; shared cosmological imagery does not yet establish shared continuity. | V12-C01 |
| E-VERAINE | **Veraine Solace** — adjacent continuity candidate | Sevenfold Theft fracture-seer; retain distinct powers until a crossover is adopted. | V12-C01 |


## Factions and internal tensions

These groupings are planning candidates, not permission to flatten entire historical peoples into one faction.


### Firstborn assemblies (F-FIRSTBORN)

Keep creation intelligible and preserve senior status. Its means include knowledge, access and interpretation. Care for younger beings competes with entitlement.

### Archonic administrations (F-ARCHONS)

Maintain a chosen order even when it requires denial. Its means include permission, naming, confinement and selective testimony. Officers know different portions of the harm they enable.

### Watchers (F-WATCHERS)

Observe and sometimes cross the boundary into participation. Its means include distance, archives and forbidden instruction. Detachment can conceal responsibility rather than avoid it.

### Covenant households (F-COVENANT-HOUSES)

Survive, inherit and interpret promises. Its means include kinship, labour, food and marriage arrangements. Household belonging can protect one person while expelling another.

### Egyptian imperial institutions (F-IMPERIAL-EGYPT)

Maintain labour, supply and royal order. Its means include bureaucracy, force, ritual and grain. Ordinary workers, officials and rulers must not become one moral silhouette.

### Wilderness assembly (F-WILDERNESS-ASSEMBLY)

Keep a displaced community alive and negotiate authority. Its means include food allocation, law, worship and collective sanction. Survival does not eliminate dissent or legitimate coercion.

### Royal houses (F-ROYAL-HOUSES)

Consolidate land, inheritance and legitimacy. Its means include taxation, courts, armies and sacred patronage. Subjects benefit unevenly; internal rivals retain their own reasons.

### Prophetic witnesses (F-PROPHETIC-WITNESSES)

Contest abuses and communicate situated visions. Its means include speech, performance, memory and risk. Sincerity is not omniscience; different witnesses can conflict.

### Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian administrations (F-IMPERIAL-CENTRES)

Different states with different aims; never a single unchanged empire. Its means include deportation, tribute, rebuilding, appointments and archives. Administrative continuity can coexist with changed rulers and changed policy.

### Diaspora communities (F-DIASPORA-COMMUNITIES)

Preserve life and belonging across changed places. Its means include language, care, trade, story and local alliances. Preservation and adaptation create real internal disagreement.

### Resistance networks (F-RESISTANCE-NETWORKS)

Resist imposed domination. Its means include secrecy, force, testimony and solidarity. Victory can reproduce the extraction it opposed.

### Jesus movement (F-JESUS-MOVEMENT)

Teach, heal, share, argue and bear witness under empire. Its means include meals, journeys, words and personal commitment. Followers disagree about risk, meaning and leadership.

### Early assemblies (F-EARLY-ASSEMBLIES)

Build communities from divergent histories and expectations. Its means include letters, hospitality, funds and competing authority claims. A letter’s remedy can become later domination when stripped of circumstance.

### Copyists and custodians (F-COPYISTS)

Carry texts through vulnerable material and political conditions. Its means include selection, copying, translation, preservation and loss. Transmission can be care, error, adaptation or control; establish evidence per case.

### Concordat (F-CONCORDAT)

Investigate and coordinate modern awakening. Its means include research, resources, secrecy and interpretation. Preparedness is not permission to direct another life.

### Coalition (F-COALITION)

Coordinate defence and repair across independent groups. Its means include shared knowledge, commitments and local competence. Cooperation can fail without making every dissenter a villain.

### Seven Thrones (F-THRONES)

Maintain their positions within the Gyre candidate continuity. Its means include interception of quintessence in sevenfold theft. Imported villain logic must not automatically redefine every biblical deity.


## Capabilities, costs and failure


### Cross-section travel

**Capability:** Move a consenting traveller into another locally lawful expression. **Conditions:** A compatible destination, an adopted route and an elapsed-time contract. **Costs:** Energy, delay, exposure and interruption of obligations. **Failure:** Failed compatibility can leave the traveller unable to embody. **Limit:** Access is not permission; nobody else’s biography is reset.

### Reincarnation / resurrection

**Capability:** A continuity may acquire renewed local expression. **Conditions:** Continuity evidence and a receiving substrate; exact mechanism unestablished. **Costs:** Lost time, changed relationships, care and uncertain recall. **Failure:** Mistaken identity, incomplete recall or inability to return. **Limit:** No guaranteed return and no cancellation of another person’s death.

### Re-cohering

**Capability:** Integrate a prior capability or memory into the present. **Conditions:** A specific recoverable state and consent to the encounter. **Costs:** Fatigue, reinterpretation and conflict with present commitments. **Failure:** Confabulation or incompatible self-states. **Limit:** Retrieval is not retroactive consent or rewriting.

### HALO practice

**Capability:** Use FLOW, MIRROR and GATE as a bounded choice grammar. **Conditions:** Three distinguished dice / domains; actual magical mechanics pending. **Costs:** Attention, commitment, risk and consequences of interpretation. **Failure:** Misreading, bias or a mismatch between intent and action. **Limit:** A roll does not override agency or prove metaphysical truth.

### Extended perception

**Capability:** Encounter information unavailable to an ordinary local perspective. **Conditions:** A declared perceptual scope and a named witness. **Costs:** Overload, uncertainty and changed responsibility. **Failure:** Confusing probability, reflection or testimony with fact. **Limit:** Perception cannot supply consent on another’s behalf.

### Naming

**Capability:** Address, distinguish or coordinate with a particular identity. **Conditions:** Enough context to distinguish source, role and incarnation. **Costs:** Exposure and responsibility for a claim made publicly. **Failure:** Misidentification, coercive naming or inherited slurs. **Limit:** A name is neither a deed of ownership nor a universal control word.

### Repair

**Capability:** Change damaged conditions through material action and accountability. **Conditions:** The harmed party’s needs and retained right to refuse reconciliation. **Costs:** Labour, resources, restitution and lost privilege. **Failure:** Performative apology, recidivism or an offered remedy that deepens harm. **Limit:** The perpetrator cannot declare the victim healed.

### Shared power

**Capability:** Coordinate separate agents without collapsing their identities. **Conditions:** Revocable agreements, visible costs and realistic shared capacity. **Costs:** Time, conflicting priorities and responsibility for dependent others. **Failure:** Capture by a leader, silent exclusion or broken commitments. **Limit:** Dissent is not proof of corruption.


## Gate functions and cultivation

The twelve gate functions are: Growth, Flux, Breath, Reflection, Radiance, Threshold, Memory, Stillness, Depth, Flame, Song, Transcendence. The last four are reported lost in an older table; neither their physical location nor their recovery is settled. No gate is automatically the realm with the same number.

The Codex ladder is Spark → Kindling → Flame → Blaze → Conflagration → Sun → Constellation. The V2 ladder is Spark-Touched → Flame-Kindled → Triple-Cast → Axis-Walker → Labyrinth-Weaver → Oracle → Crown. No equivalence between their individual stages is asserted.


## Glossary


### Omnoid

The approved larger cosmological frame. The diagram shows conceptual relations, not a scientific model.

### Cross-section

A locally experienced world or moment within the larger frame; its exact geometry is not yet adopted.

### Worldline

The ordered sequence a being or community lives through. A later return does not delete earlier experience.

### Source

An originating identity or principle. A source is not interchangeable with every expression attributed to it.

### Aspect

A particular relational or functional expression of a source, indexed separately from the whole.

### Manifestation

A local appearance or acting presence. Its claimed source may be accurate, mistaken or deceptive.

### Incarnation

An embodied life with its own biography and agency, even when continuity with another life is established.

### Identity claim

A proposition about who someone is. Names, resemblance and memories are evidence to examine, not automatic proof.

### Continuity

What persists across changes of embodiment. The project has not adopted a universal test for proving it.

### Aura

The outward expression of spirit in the Omnoid source vocabulary; not a diagnostic claim about real people.

### Soul

The inward continuity vocabulary of the cosmology; its status here is literary/metaphysical, not measured physical substance.

### Machine layer

The Omnoid source’s term for local form and the conversion between intention and expression; not necessarily metal machinery.

### Flesh

The vulnerable embodied surface. Cosmic significance does not prevent bodily pain, hunger or exhaustion.

### Bone

The structural layer of embodiment in the inherited vocabulary; not an exact anatomical system for every realm.

### Throat

The proposed passage where inward and outward expression meet. It is not a route through another’s consent.

### Substrate

The local conditions in which a being can take form; different settings may require different lawful expression.

### Re-crystallization

The inherited term for forming a local expression again. Its available mechanisms and costs remain proposals.

### Re-cohering

Recovering or integrating something into the present without erasing the intervening history.

### Selective retroactivity

An inherited phrase requiring care: this project interprets it as present integration, not the power to overwrite another life.

### Realm

A traversable or experienceable domain. It is not automatically a gate function or a stage of personal growth.

### Fundament

Baseline embodied reality in the Unraveling vocabulary; the relationship to historical Earth is a candidate mapping.

### Threshold

Liminal geography. The similarly named gate function is a different indexed category.

### Labyrinth

The domain of choices and alternatives in V2; encountering alternatives does not erase the enacted path.

### Reflection

The realm of contested self-perception; also a separately indexed gate function and a common word.

### Engine

The V2 domain of local reality’s mechanisms. It is not the whole Omnoid or every being’s Machine layer.

### Web

Navigable relations. Connected people remain separate agents with different obligations.

### Sight

A realm and a capacity concerned with perception. Neither guarantees truth or sound judgment.

### Crown

A realm and a V2 cultivation label. Their shared name does not establish identical meaning.

### Gate function

One of the Codex’s twelve operative names: a function that may occur in multiple places.

### Lost domain

A domain reported missing in an older draft. Destroyed, inaccessible and hidden are different states.

### HALO

Hidden Axis Labyrinthine Oracle: a three-domain symbolic system inherited from existing drafts.

### FLOW

HALO’s movement domain, containing eight named faces.

### MIRROR

HALO’s reflection domain, containing eight named faces; not the same entity as the Reflection realm.

### GATE

HALO’s choice and boundary domain, containing eight named faces; distinct from twelve gate functions.

### Symbol

One named face. There are twenty-four across the three distinguished dice.

### Ordered triple

One FLOW result, one MIRROR result and one GATE result in that domain order: 8 × 8 × 8 = 512 possibilities.

### Cultivation

A vocabulary of acquired capacities and obligations. Existing ladders are preserved without declaring stage-by-stage equivalence.

### The Mother

A primordial source candidate in the Codex. Lilith, Mary and every mother are not automatically the same person.

### First Flame

A creative consciousness in existing drafts. A lightbearing descendant is not identical merely because both involve light.

### Firstborn

Divine children in the inherited mythology; seniority does not grant ownership of later beings.

### Archon

An authority figure or administration in the selected literary cosmology; historical traditions using this term require separate notes.

### Watchers

A grouping whose observation and involvement vary by source; 1 Enoch must not be silently merged with every angel tradition.

### Hollow

An unresolved draft concept spanning entropy, loneliness and damaged relation. Do not equate mental illness with moral corruption.

### Architect

A role with competing occupant histories in Unraveling. Eve’s identification is a V2 proposal, not settled series canon.

### Quintessence

The Five-Aspect soul-matter vocabulary of Sevenfold Theft; a neighbouring candidate system, not silently imported physics.

### Gyre

The Sevenfold candidate’s cyclical world structure. Similarity to Omnoid imagery is insufficient to prove a shared setting.

### Wolfspace

Pocket-dimension vocabulary from the in-world academic paper. Its equations are not treated as established mathematics or science.

### Agency

A being’s capacity and standing to choose, refuse and act. Characters can violate it; the story records the consequences.

### Consent

Specific, informed, revocable agreement. Silence, identity continuity or another version’s agreement is not a substitute.

### Harm

Damage to a person or community, including coerced loss of agency; good intentions do not erase effects.

### Responsibility

Answerability for choices and their effects, including the work required after unintended harm.

### Repair

Material and relational work shaped by those harmed. It is different from demanding forgiveness.

### Forgiveness

A possible choice belonging to the harmed party. It cannot be charged as the price of restitution.

### Source-story order

The sequence in a particular text or the proposed braided outline; it does not itself establish historical dates.

### Historical date

An independently supported period or range. Unknown remains unknown, rather than being back-calculated from symbolic ages.

### Composition date

When a text or layer was written. Daniel’s narrated exile setting does not date the composition automatically.

### Realm time

The clock adopted inside a domain, with no conversion until a relation is explicitly established.

### Personal time

A character’s experienced duration, including intervals different from an outside observer’s calendar.

### First-safe chapter

The earliest proposed reader access to a fact. It is spoiler management, not the date of the underlying event.

### Lasting consequence

A changed condition carried into later scenes: a death, debt, disability, migration, promise, destroyed home or broken trust.


## Source and authority notes

The source paths and bounded external references are recorded in [world data](/codex-apockalypsis/files/world.json). The existing Codex, Unraveling and Sevenfold manuscripts are source witnesses for **literary content**, not evidence of author adoption or historical truth. Omnoid source details beyond the approved larger frame remain candidates.

See [the chronology](/codex-apockalypsis/library/reference-world-chronology), [the atlas guide](/codex-apockalypsis/library/atlas-readme), and the internal reconciliation (unpublished source reference).
